rules.title: Use a 4/8 spacing scale
rules.why: Values drawn from one scale give every screen the same rhythm, while one-off numbers make layouts look accidental.
do: Take every padding, margin and gap from a token scale such as 4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48.
Use padding for space inside an element and gap or margin for space between elements, both from the same scale.
Give repeated elements (cards, rows, chips) identical spacing.
Apply the scale to padding, margins, gaps and component sizes; 1px borders, 2px focus outlines, line heights and 1-2px optical icon nudges sit outside it.
avoid: Off-scale values such as 7, 13 or 22px, or different inner padding on sibling cards.
rules.note: A 4px base and an 8px base are both fine; pick one and enforce it.

rules.title: Let spacing show what belongs together
rules.why: People read small gaps as "related" and large gaps as "separate", so spacing can carry structure without borders or labels.
do: Use tiers: about 4-8px between a label and its own input, 12-16px between items in a group, 24-32px between groups, and 40-48px between independent sections.
Keep every label clearly closer to its own field than to the field above it.
Leave the largest gap in a form just before the primary action, and keep qualifying text (for example consent text) close to the button it qualifies.
avoid: One uniform gap between labels, fields, buttons and sections.
Label placement that floats halfway between two inputs.

rules.title: Give content room to breathe
rules.why: Cramped layouts are hard to scan and tap; adding space is often the fastest way to make a busy screen calm.
do: Keep at least 16px between text and container edges, and 24px on roomy mobile cards.
Give every card in a set the same inner padding on all sides.
When a screen feels busy, try doubling the gaps inside cards and between sections before removing content.
avoid: Text or buttons touching card edges, or tight 4px gaps between headings and their content.
Spacing so large that related items stop looking related.
Lopsided sections with text in one half and nothing in the other, or empty bands from stacked section padding and margins.

rules.title: Align to shared edges
rules.why: Near-miss alignment of a few pixels reads as sloppiness even when users cannot say why.
do: Align icons, text and buttons in a column to one left edge, and align numeric values such as prices to one right edge.
In card rows, make cards equal height and pin the action to the bottom (flex column with margin-top: auto) so buttons share a baseline.
Inspect layouts at high zoom or with guides to catch 1-6px offsets.
Left-align text by default; center only short moments such as a one- or two-line hero, an empty state or a short dialog.
avoid: Centered body paragraphs next to left-aligned headings in the same block, or centered paragraphs longer than about three lines.

rules.title: One focal point per screen
rules.why: When every element has the same weight, users do not know where to look first.
do: Rank content with size, weight and color: one large title, quieter body text and one high-contrast primary action.

Run a squint test (filter: blur(6px) on the page root, or a screenshot shrunk to about 25%): the primary action should still be the most distinct shape; if several compete, quiet the secondary fills before enlarging the primary.
Vary emphasis deliberately, for example a featured card larger than regular ones.
avoid: Headline, body and button text at similar size and weight.
A loud primary button repeated on every row of a list.
Rows of three or more identical icon-title-blurb cards with no lead item; keep uniform tiles for genuinely comparable items such as products or search results.

rules.title: Remove elements that do not earn their place
rules.why: Every element competes for attention, so extras slow users down on the main task.
do: For each element, ask which user task it supports; remove or move it if the answer is none.
Move secondary details into detail views or disclosures.
Consolidate scattered secondary actions into one clearly placed control.
avoid: Decorative icons, duplicate buttons, "see all" links and filler added just because there is space.
Simplifying by fading the remaining text below 4.5:1 or replacing labeled primary navigation with a single icon button.
rules.note: Never remove information people need to decide or act, such as price, limits, errors or legal text.

rules.title: Group with space and tint before borders
rules.why: Every line adds visual noise; spacing and subtle background tints group content more quietly.
do: Separate list rows with consistent spacing instead of a divider under every item.

Give inputs such as search a light filled background instead of a box inside another bordered band, and keep the field identifiable with a border or bottom edge at 3:1 or more against its surroundings.
Set off footers or action bars with a faint background tint.
avoid: Stacking borders, bands and outlines on the same element.
A near-white fill (about 1.1:1) as the only cue that an input exists.
rules.note: Dense data tables can still benefit from row separators.

rules.title: Lay out on a column grid
rules.why: A shared grid makes widths and gutters repeat, so edges line up across rows and screens.
do: Use about 4 columns on mobile, 8 on tablet and 12 on desktop, with fixed gutters such as 16px.
Size cards and tiles to whole columns, using CSS Grid or a layout primitive rather than hand-set widths.
avoid: Arbitrary component widths that share no edges, or gutters that change between rows of one layout.

rules.title: Chunk long content and disclose progressively
rules.why: Working memory is limited; short labeled sections are easier to scan than a wall of text.
do: Break long content into short titled sections with numbers or icons.
Show a one-line summary on detail cards and put secondary details in collapsible rows.
Keep the primary action visible after the summary, not after all the text.
avoid: Hiding information needed for the decision (price, key specs) inside collapsed sections.

rules.title: Keep text and images in separate tracks
rules.why: Text that wraps around a small inline image keeps changing line length, which breaks reading rhythm.
do: Put the image full width above or below the paragraph, or give image and text their own columns.
Stack image above text on narrow screens.
avoid: Floating a small image inside a paragraph so lines are short beside it and long below it.

rules.title: Let feature media break out of the text column
rules.why: In long-form pages, images wider than the reading column add rhythm and immersion while text keeps a comfortable measure.
do: Define grid tracks for a narrow text column plus wider "breakout" and "full-bleed" tracks for media.
Keep body text at a readable measure while hero and key images use the wider tracks.
avoid: Forcing every image in a long article to the narrow text width.
rules.note: Optional technique for editorial layouts.

rules.title: Vary image sizes in editorial galleries
rules.why: A few larger images give the eye an entry point; a wall of identical thumbnails has none.
do: Let the lead image span a full row or a 2x2 block, with smaller images around it, using grid-column and grid-row spans.
Put the strongest image in the largest slot and keep gutters uniform.
avoid: Mixed sizes in product listings, where uniform tiles are better for comparison.

rules.title: Spacing recipe for a single-question mobile step
rules.why: One-field steps (email, name, code) look calm and structured when every gap follows a deliberate rhythm.
do: On a 375pt-wide frame, place a 56pt navigation row with a 44x44 back target directly under the runtime top inset, then a title of about 28px about 8px below it, with 8px to its description.
Leave 24px to a 56px-tall full-width input with 16px side margins and a visible label above it, or a floating label that stays visible once filled.
Put a related secondary link 16px below the input, then a large gap before the bottom group.
Keep consent text 24px above a 56px full-width primary button that sits 16px above the keyboard or safe area.
avoid: Using the same gap within and between groups, a top offset hard-coded to one status-bar height, or letting the button touch the keyboard.
rules.note: Scale the values proportionally for other device sizes; read safe areas at runtime.

rules.title: Bento grids need one leading tile
rules.why: Mixed-size tiles read as one system only when gaps, radii and padding are identical and one tile clearly leads.
do: Lay out with CSS Grid (for example repeat(12, 1fr) or grid-template-areas) and let tiles span columns and rows.
Use one gap value, one radius token and one inner padding for every tile.
Give exactly one tile the lead (larger, or the only accent fill) and collapse to a single column with that tile first on mobile.
avoid: Several radii, gaps or shadow styles on one screen, or several bright tiles competing for attention.

rules.title: Adapt the layout to each device class
rules.why: Stretching a phone layout to desktop wastes space, and shrinking a desktop layout onto a phone crowds it.
do: Switch patterns at breakpoints or container queries (around 600px and 1024px): phone with one column and bottom navigation, tablet with a side rail and two panes, desktop with a sidebar and multi-column grid.
Keep components and tokens shared across breakpoints so it still reads as one product.
Let tile groups reflow by available width, for example repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 10rem), 1fr)), so four tiles become two per row before one.
For split layouts such as sign-in beside an illustration, drop or shrink the visual on mobile so the form comes first.
avoid: Proportionally shrinking a desktop split layout onto a phone.

rules.title: Scale spacing from a reference design, never the user's text size
rules.why: Scaling lengths from a reference frame keeps proportions, but text must still follow the user's accessibility settings.
do: Use flexible layout primitives (flex, grid, constraints) for structure and scale only spacing and radii if needed.
If a reference-frame scaler is used, compute its factor from the shorter screen side and clamp it to about 0.85-1.2, so tablets, landscape and split screen gain content rather than oversized chrome.
Respect the platform text scale (for example MediaQuery textScaler, allowFontScaling or rem units) and clamp only extreme values, for example with maxFontSizeMultiplier on dense UI.
avoid: Shrinking all fonts with screen width, applying a layout scale factor to font sizes, or assuming one phone size fits tablets and split screen.
rules.note: Pixel-scaling helpers are debated; responsive layout is the better default.

rules.title: Build layouts that survive translation and right-to-left
rules.why: Fixed widths, physical left and right properties and one overflow rule for everything break as soon as text grows or direction flips.
do: Size labeled controls with min-width and padding, and plan for about 30% longer sentences and two to three times longer short labels.
Use logical properties (margin-inline-start, padding-inline, inset-inline-end, text-align: start) and set lang and dir on the root element.
Mirror directional icons such as back arrows and chevrons in right-to-left layouts, but not logos, clocks, media playback symbols or numbers.
Choose overflow by element type: buttons grow or go full width rather than clip, table cells truncate with the full text available, and titles clamp to two lines.
avoid: Fixed widths on buttons, tabs or chips that hold translated text.
overflow: hidden as a global default, or margin-left and padding-right in components that must flip.
rules.note: Test with a long-word language and a right-to-left language before shipping.

rules.title: Use one or two typefaces and build hierarchy inside them
rules.why: Several unrelated typefaces look improvised; one family varied by size, weight and color stays coherent.
do: Use the platform system stack (system-ui, -apple-system, Roboto) or one neutral, well-hinted UI sans for body, labels and buttons.
Reserve any expressive display face for large headlines, if at all.
Load only the weights in use, subset fonts, use font-display: swap and keep a system fallback stack.
Check the font license before bundling, keep the license file with self-hosted copies, and self-host for privacy-sensitive products, since third-party font servers receive every visitor's IP address.
avoid: Mixing script, serif and sans faces within one card or heading, including a single italic-serif accent word in a sans headline, unless the brand system defines that treatment.
Monospace as a decorative "technical" voice for navigation, labels or marketing figures; reserve it for code, identifiers and keyboard keys, and use tabular-nums when figures must align.
Decorative faces for paragraphs, form labels or button text.

rules.title: Keep a short type scale
rules.why: Many slightly different font sizes read as noise; a few deliberate steps create clear levels.
do: Define about 5-6 sizes as tokens or utility classes, each with a fixed line height and weight, for example Display 32, Title 24, Heading 18, Body 16, Secondary 14, and Caption 12-13 only for captions, field labels and metadata.
Start from platform ramps where they apply (iOS body 17pt, Android body 16sp, web body 16px) and step headings with a ratio of about 1.2-1.25.

On iOS, take sizes from the Dynamic Type text styles (for example Large Title 34, Title 1 28, Body 17, Subheadline 15, Footnote 13, Caption 12pt) and apply them with .font(.body) or preferredFont(forTextStyle:), so they follow the user's text-size setting.
Audit computed sizes on the rendered page at phone and desktop widths: more than about 8 distinct sizes (about 10 in a dense app) signals drift, so merge strays into the nearest step.
avoid: Sizes outside the scale, two sizes within 2px doing different jobs, or 1px nudges used to fix layout problems.
rules.note: Data-dense apps may need one or two extra steps, but every size still comes from the scale.

rules.title: Match weight to size and avoid thin weights
rules.why: Thin and light weights look elegant but are hard to read at small sizes and on poor screens.
do: Use Regular (400) as the minimum for body text and labels.
Use Semibold or Bold (600-700) for headings and button labels.
avoid: Weights 100-300 for body text or small labels, especially combined with light gray.
Long passages of small text set in bold.

rules.title: Keep text sizes readable on mobile
rules.why: Tiny text slows scanning and excludes people with low vision.
do: Keep body text at the platform default or larger (iOS 17pt, Android 16sp, web 16px).
Treat about 14px as the floor for list items and secondary text, and 12px as the floor for small field labels.
Use 16px for web form inputs so mobile browsers do not zoom on focus.
avoid: 8-10px labels or list text, especially in pale gray.

rules.title: Limit line length and set comfortable line height
rules.why: Very long lines make it hard to find the next line; tight leading makes paragraphs dense.
do: Cap body text at about 45-75 characters per line (for example max-width: 65ch).
Use a line height of about 1.4-1.6 for paragraphs, about 1.2-1.35 for one- or two-line labels, list titles and card titles, and 1.1-1.3 for large headings.
Let layouts survive the WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.12 text-spacing overrides (line height 1.5, paragraph spacing 2em, letter spacing 0.12em, word spacing 0.16em) without clipping or overlap.
avoid: Paragraphs that stretch across the full width of wide screens, or fixed heights on text containers.

rules.title: Leave body tracking alone and use capitals sparingly
rules.why: Extra letter spacing breaks up word shapes, and long runs of capitals are slow to read.
do: Keep letter-spacing at the font default for body text.
Use uppercase only for short eyebrows, tags and overlines, set smaller with about +0.05-0.1em tracking, applied with text-transform so screen readers do not spell words out.
Use slight negative tracking only on very large display headings, if needed.
Add an eyebrow only when it states a fact the heading lacks (a category, step or status); keep it at 12px or larger and 4.5:1, de-emphasized by size, case and tracking rather than a lighter gray.
avoid: Widened tracking on paragraphs, headlines and paragraphs in all caps, or an eyebrow above every section that repeats its heading.

rules.title: Make headings darker than body text
rules.why: A near-black, heavier heading above a slightly lighter body creates an instant reading order.
do: Set titles in the strongest text color token and a heavier weight.
Set supporting text in a medium gray that still reaches at least 4.5:1 on every surface it appears on: the lightest passing gray is about #767676 on white, #737373 on #FAFAFA and #6E6E6E on #F2F2F2.
avoid: Titles in the same light gray as body copy, or low-contrast gray for errors and other critical messages.
Relative specs such as "50% lighter", or a secondary gray checked only on white (#6B7280 is 4.8:1 on white but 4.4:1 on #F3F4F6; iOS secondaryLabel is about 3.4:1 on white).

rules.title: Style same-role text identically
rules.why: When all prices, dates or labels look the same, users learn the pattern once.
do: Define named text styles (eyebrow, H1, H2, body, caption, price) and apply them everywhere.
Give every value with the same role the same size, weight and color.
avoid: Coloring each highlighted word or price differently for variety.

rules.title: Set numbers for comparison
rules.why: In finance and dashboard views the figures are the content, and they must align and compare at a glance.
do: Use font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums and right-align amounts in lists and tables.
Keep one decimal precision per column, and set currency symbols and units slightly smaller than the number.
Pair a large key figure with its unit and a plain qualifier ("120 bpm, normal"), plus a gauge or range when thresholds matter.
avoid: Lone numbers with no unit or meaning, or mixed precision within one column.

rules.title: Keep text as real, selectable text
rules.why: Text drawn into images, canvas or CSS content is hard to select, translate, search or read aloud.
do: Put headings, messages and receipts in HTML, and use CSS only to style them.
Layer decorative canvas or 3D effects behind or above real text with pointer-events: none.
avoid: User-facing messages in ::before or ::after content, or receipts and confirmations rendered as flat images.

rules.title: Use display and novelty type only as accents
rules.why: Oversized, condensed, dot-matrix or split-word type adds energy but loses legibility quickly.
do: Limit display type to short headlines (2-5 words) sized with clamp(), for example clamp(3rem, 10vw, 10rem), with line-height around 0.9-1.
Use novelty numerals only for one or two large figures (32px or more), keep their own dots or strokes at 3:1 or better, and keep a plain label beside them at 4.5:1.
When a headline is split or partly muted for effect, keep the full text as the accessible name and keep the muted part at 3:1 or better.
avoid: Display or dot-matrix faces for body text, small labels, tables or placeholders.
Display type over busy photography without a scrim.

rules.title: Measure contrast against WCAG AA
rules.why: Text that looks fine to the designer can be unreadable for people with low vision or in bright light.
do: Reach at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (24px+, or 18.66px+ bold).
Treat 14-17px button labels, badges and captions as normal text even when semibold, so a white label needs a fill dark enough for 4.5:1 (white on #007AFF is only 4.0:1; #0070E0 reaches 4.8:1).
Reach at least 3:1 for UI component boundaries, focus indicators and icons that carry meaning.
Check every token pair with a contrast tool, including white labels on brand-colored buttons, and recompute any ratio written on a spec instead of trusting it.
avoid: Judging contrast by eye, or pale brand text on a light tint of the same hue.
rules.note: A bright brand color does not guarantee readable white text; many oranges, greens and cyans fail with white.

rules.title: Start neutral and give one accent a job
rules.why: When everything is colorful nothing stands out; a neutral base lets the accent signal importance.
do: Lay out the screen in neutrals first, then add color only where it carries meaning: primary action, links, active state, status.
Work from a compact palette: a light base, a dark base, one accent and at most one supporting tone.
Keep structural colors (surfaces, text) separate from semantic colors (success, warning, error).
avoid: A different pastel or gradient on every card, banner and icon.
Using the accent on headings, icons, bullets, borders or decorative shapes until it no longer signals interactivity.

rules.title: Use 60-30-10 as a starting balance
rules.why: A rough split between base, secondary and accent color keeps a screen calm and the accent meaningful.
do: Aim for about 60% neutral base, 30% secondary surfaces and 10% accent, judged by visual weight.
Define the three roles as tokens (for example --color-bg, --color-surface, --color-accent).
Count accent roles as well as area: a screen near 10% can still dilute the accent across buttons, tabs, deltas and chart bars, so give deltas status tokens and chart highlights their own token.
avoid: Spreading the accent across large backgrounds.
rules.note: A heuristic, not a quota.

rules.title: Give the most important action the strongest color
rules.why: The eye lands first on the most saturated, highest-contrast element.
do: Give the single most important action the most vivid fill on the screen and keep surrounding controls muted.
On dark screens, use a bold filled call to action rather than an outlined one that blends in.
avoid: Several equally vivid elements competing, or a muted primary action beside vivid decoration.

rules.title: Avoid pure primaries and pure black on white for large areas
rules.why: Fully saturated hues and maximal contrast across large surfaces look harsh and tire the eyes.
do: Use slightly toned variants instead of #FF0000, #00FF00, #0000FF and similar pure hues.
Use near-black (for example #171717) for text and dark surfaces and an off-white for large light backgrounds.

Store the chosen values as tokens and verify each text pairing still meets contrast minimums; toning a hue down does not make white labels readable by itself, so pair light tones with near-black text.
avoid: Pure #000000 text on pure #FFFFFF across large reading areas.

rules.title: Reserve status colors for status
rules.why: If red and green appear decoratively, users misread them as errors or success.
do: Keep red for errors and destructive actions, green for success and amber for warnings, applied consistently across the product.
Pair every status color with an icon and explicit wording.

Split each status color into a text token of at least 4.5:1 for status words and percentages (green #15803D is about 5.0:1 on white) and a brighter token of at least 3:1 for icons, bars and dots (#16A34A, about 3.3:1); mid greens such as #22C55E (about 2.3:1) fail even as icons.
avoid: Brand or decorative elements in the error red or success green, or active states such as tab underlines and secondary buttons in the error red.

rules.title: Never rely on color alone
rules.why: Color-blind users, low-vision users and anyone in bright light can miss color-only cues.
do: Add a second cue to every color-coded meaning: text, icon, shape, weight or position.
Keep status words inside status badges and check marks on selected items.
avoid: Red borders as the only error signal, or color-only active states and chart series.

rules.title: Protect text placed over images
rules.why: Text over photos becomes unreadable wherever the image is bright or busy.
do: Add a scrim behind overlaid text, such as linear-gradient(to top, rgba(0,0,0,.6), transparent) across the lower third, or in light themes a white fade that is fully opaque under near-black text.
Check contrast against the lightest part of the image behind the text, sizing the scrim for the brightest image in the set and testing it with the smallest caption.
Apply the same check to header and navigation links that sit over a hero.
Put small overlays such as ratings on solid pills.
avoid: White text straight on skies, buildings, mid-tone or busy areas, or a text shadow as the only protection for small text.

rules.title: Collapse near-duplicate colors into tokens
rules.why: Five grays a few RGB steps apart are values that drifted off the system; they cause inconsistency and maintenance pain.
do: Define a small set of named tokens (text-primary, text-secondary, border, surface) and reference only those.
Search stylesheets for raw hex values and merge near-duplicates into the nearest token.
When merging grays used for text, round toward the darker value so it keeps 4.5:1 on off-white surfaces too; #767676 is the lightest gray that passes on pure white.
avoid: Hard-coded one-off colors inside components.

rules.title: Keep focus and pending colors apart from verdict colors
rules.why: When red and green appear only for results, users read success and failure instantly; tinting focus or waiting states the same way misleads.
do: Show focus, progress and waiting states with a neutral or brand color, using lightness, an outline or a glow.
Switch to the success or error token only once the result is known, and pair it with an icon and text.
avoid: A red outline on a merely focused field, or green and red tints on states that are still pending.

rules.title: Check text on accent fills and gradients
rules.why: Light accents such as lime, yellow, orange and cyan often fail with white text, and gradients fail at their lightest stop.
do: Define an on-accent text token for each accent from the fill's relative luminance: white reaches 4.5:1 only up to about 0.18 (about as dark as #767676 gray), so lighter fills get near-black text.
Check the label on every state's fill (default, hover, pressed, busy, progress), since lighter hover and busy shades are where white labels usually fail.

For white labels on common 50-900 color ramps, expect to need the 700 step for green, emerald, teal, cyan, orange and amber and at least the 600 step for blue, indigo, violet and red (for example #15803D, #C2410C, #2563EB, #DC2626); otherwise keep the bright fill and switch the label to near-black.
Check labels against the lightest stop of any gradient, and darken the stops or switch text color until it passes.

For gradient-filled text (background-clip: text), declare a solid color first as a fallback, check the lightest stop against the background (3:1 for large text, 4.5:1 otherwise), and switch to solid text for print and under @media (forced-colors: active).
When accents are sampled from imagery or brand material, darken or lighten them until text reaches 4.5:1 against the real background.
avoid: White text on lime, yellow, orange, mint, teal or mid-blue fills, or a gradient button whose label fades out at one end.

rules.title: Give translucent surfaces a contrast floor
rules.why: Text on frosted or translucent panels changes contrast with whatever sits behind it.
do: Pair backdrop-filter blur (about 12-24px) with a semi-opaque tint and a 1px light border, and raise the tint until the faintest text tier (secondary text, timestamps) passes 4.5:1 against the worst-case background.
When the backdrop can be anything, use at least about 55% black under white text or about 50% white under near-black text, because blur alone leaves large bright or dark areas intact.
Set secondary text on glass at about 80% opacity or more, or use a solid token.

Write -webkit-backdrop-filter beside backdrop-filter, and provide an opaque fallback under @supports not ((backdrop-filter: blur(1px)) or (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1px))) and @media (prefers-reduced-transparency: reduce).
Use regular or medium weights for small text and keep the number of stacked blurred layers low.
avoid: Secondary text or placeholders at 30-60% white on glass over photos or video.
rules.note: If shapes behind the panel are still recognizable under the text, the blur and tint are too weak.

rules.title: Change the fill, not the ink, for errors on colored controls
rules.why: Red text on a colored button can drop near 1:1 contrast, while a red fill with white text stays readable.
do: Switch the control's background token to the error color and keep the foreground white or near-black as needed.
Pair the color change with an icon and a short caption.
avoid: Recoloring only the label or icon red on a colored button.

rules.title: Keep category tints soft and consistent
rules.why: Pastel backgrounds can separate categories quietly if the mapping is stable and text stays readable.
do: Assign each category one pastel background with dark text and reuse the mapping in every tile, card and panel.
Pair the tint with a label or icon so the category is clear without color.
avoid: Mid-gray text on pastel fills, or a category color that changes between views.

rules.title: Build dark mode as its own palette, not an inversion
rules.why: Inverting light colors produces glare and broken hierarchy; a dark theme needs its own tuned values.
do: Implement themes by remapping semantic color tokens per mode, so components need no theme-specific code.
Keep brand hues recognizable but retune their lightness and saturation for dark surfaces.
avoid: Automatic inversion of the light palette, or hard-coded colors that force separate dark components.

rules.title: Use a near-black base, not pure black
rules.why: Dark gray reduces harsh contrast and leaves room to show depth with lighter surfaces.
do: Use a near-black base such as #121212, or a dark tinted toward the brand hue at about the same lightness (such as #110F1B).
Fill cards with a slightly lighter surface rather than outlining them.
avoid: Pure #000000 backgrounds, #000000 cards on #000000 backgrounds, or "colored blacks" so dark (such as #03000D) that they look and behave like pure black.
rules.note: A true-black option can suit OLED-focused media apps; offer it as a setting, not the default.

rules.title: Show elevation with lighter surfaces
rules.why: Shadows barely show on dark backgrounds, so lightness must communicate which layer is on top.
do: Step surfaces lighter as they rise, for example base #121212, card #1E1E1E, app bar #272727, menu #2E2E2E, dialog #383838.
Expose these as elevation tokens so components pick the right surface automatically.
avoid: One dark color for background, cards and dialogs, or black drop shadows as the only separation.

rules.title: Use dimmed whites for text tiers
rules.why: Pure white on near-black glares; graded off-whites keep reading comfortable and preserve hierarchy.
do: Define text tiers as white alpha over the current surface: about 87% for primary text, 60% for secondary text and 38% only for disabled elements (#E0E0E0, #A0A0A0 and #6C6C6C on #121212).

If tiers are fixed or hue-tinted grays, check each on the lightest surface it can sit on: #A0A0A0 passes from #121212 to #2E2E2E but falls below 4.5:1 on a #383838 dialog, which needs about #AAAAAA or lighter.

Keep all text people read, including placeholders, captions, timestamps, chart ticks and inactive tab labels, at 4.5:1 or more; on near-black bases that means no dimmer than about #808080, and 60% white is the safer floor.
avoid: Long body text in pure #FFFFFF at bold weight on a dark base.
Gray hexes tuned on the base surface and reused unchanged in menus and dialogs, or meta text in the disabled tier or thin weights, which commonly falls to 2-3:1.
rules.note: The 38% tier is about 3.6:1 on #121212; it is acceptable only for disabled controls, which WCAG exempts.

rules.title: Retune accent colors for dark surfaces
rules.why: A brand color tuned for white backgrounds often loses contrast or vibrates on dark ones.
do: Define separate dark-theme accent tokens, usually lighter and less saturated tones of the brand hue: one for fills and a lighter one for accent-colored text such as links, active tabs and outlined-button labels.

Check the button fill against the surface (at least 3:1) and the label against the fill (at least 4.5:1); once the accent fill is light, switch its label to a near-black on-accent token (white on #7FA6E8 is about 2.5:1, near-black about 7.5:1).
Soften semantic colors the same way: on #121212, red #DC2626 is about 3.9:1 and fails for small text, while #F87171 reaches about 6.8:1.
Check accent and status text on every elevation step it can appear on, not only the base: #CF6679 is 5.2:1 on #121212 but about 3.3:1 on a #383838 dialog.
avoid: Reusing the saturated light-theme brand color unchanged, or deep 600-900 tones that sink into dark cards.
White labels on a lightened accent fill, or one accent token used for both fills and small text.

rules.title: Keep interactive states visible on dark surfaces
rules.why: Subtle hover and pressed changes that work on white often vanish on dark backgrounds.
do: Give buttons and links a clear hover and pressed change: a color shift, inversion, border or icon motion.
Show a 2px or thicker high-contrast focus ring on every focusable element, drawn with outline and outline-offset rather than box-shadow alone, which forced-colors mode removes.
avoid: A tiny opacity change as the only hover cue, or removed focus outlines.

rules.title: Let people choose the theme
rules.why: Preference for light or dark varies by person and context.
do: Default to the system setting (prefers-color-scheme) and offer a Light / Dark / System choice that persists.
Build colors as semantic tokens so both themes stay in sync.
avoid: Dark-only or light-only products with no way to switch.

rules.title: Check every screen in both themes
rules.why: Assets designed only against white, such as dark logos and shadows, silently break in dark mode.
do: Review every screen end to end in dark mode before shipping.
Provide a light logo variant or an SVG that uses currentColor.
Ship dark variants of illustrations and dim bright photographs slightly in the dark theme (for example filter: brightness(.9)).
Replace shadow-based separation with lighter surfaces or borders in the dark theme.

Give embedded frames and players a container in the surface color, set color-scheme on the embedding page, and reveal the iframe on its load event (or show a dark poster first) so it never flashes white.
avoid: A black logo disappearing on a dark card.
Headlines or hero copy fixed to white and carried into the light theme; route their color through the theme's text token.

rules.title: Separate dark surfaces with hairlines and one bright primary
rules.why: On near-black screens, depth reads best from lighter surfaces and faint borders, and one bright action anchors the screen.
do: Separate cards and popovers with 1px borders at about 6-12% white in addition to lighter surface steps; use alpha white so one border token works on every surface.
Give inputs, outlined buttons and other control boundaries at least 3:1 against the surface (about #656565 on #18181B), since hairlines reach only about 1.2-1.5:1.
Make the primary action a light or single-accent fill and keep secondary actions outlined or ghost.
Raise small label grays until they reach 4.5:1.
avoid: Several competing accents on one dark screen, or light-theme drop shadows used as the elevation cue.
Card hairlines reused as the outline of inputs or outlined buttons.

rules.title: Name the theme toggle and tune each theme
rules.why: A theme switch must say what it does, and effects tuned for one theme rarely work unchanged in the other.
do: Make the toggle a button with role="switch" and aria-checked, or aria-pressed, plus a visible label or accessible name naming the mode.
Default to prefers-color-scheme, persist the choice, and swap a full token set (text, surfaces, CTA, glows, shadows) per theme.
Re-check hero text and primary button contrast in every theme.
avoid: Icon-only toggles without a name, or one CTA color that loses contrast in the other theme.

rules.title: Keep theme transitions brief and optional
rules.why: A transition that grows from the toggle links cause and effect, but it must never slow the switch down.
do: Wrap the theme change in document.startViewTransition() and animate ::view-transition-new(root) from clip-path: circle(0 at x y) to circle(r at x y) at the toggle's center, with r = Math.hypot() to the farthest viewport corner.
Give the keyframes both a start and an end circle so the reveal does not snap, and set animation: none on ::view-transition-old(root) so the old snapshot does not crossfade.
Ease the radius out over about 300-400ms so most of the screen changes early, and keep the whole reveal under about 500ms.
Swap instantly when the API is missing or prefers-reduced-motion is set, and update the toggle's own state and label immediately.
avoid: Full-screen overlays that block input during the change.
Reveals of 600ms or longer, or a linear radius that leaves most of the screen unswitched until late.

rules.title: One primary action per view, with a clear hierarchy
rules.why: Users should spot the main action instantly; secondary and tertiary styles support it instead of competing.
do: Style the primary action as a solid fill in the accent color, one per view or section.
Style secondary actions as outlined or neutral filled buttons (for example a light gray fill with near-black text, or a pale accent tint with dark accent text), and minor actions as text buttons.
Lower emphasis only through fill and border (filled, then outlined or neutral, then text), and keep every enabled label at 4.5:1 or more.
Keep height, radius and type identical across levels so only emphasis changes, and repeat the same mapping on every repeated card.
Keep Cancel and Back neutral rather than red, and give a destructive action that sits beside Save an outlined or text style, set apart from it.
avoid: Two filled primary buttons side by side, or a different saturated color on each button.
Switching which action is filled between cards in the same list.
A secondary made from a lighter tint of the primary with the white label kept, or gray, faded labels that make enabled buttons look disabled.

rules.title: Design every state of every button
rules.why: Visible states tell users what is interactive, what is happening and what is unavailable.
do: Define default, hover, pressed, focus-visible, disabled and loading states for every variant, including icon-only buttons.
Derive hover, focus and pressed from one formula, such as an overlay of the label color at about 8% for hover and 10-12% for focus and pressed, or one or two steps darker on the color ramp.
Give each state's fill its own on-color label token, switched together with the fill, and check every pair; with white labels, darken on hover rather than lighten.

Draw focus as outline: 2px solid with outline-offset: 2px in a color that reaches at least 3:1 against the surrounding background (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11), with a two-tone ring (light inside, dark outside) on colored or image surfaces, and add it without switching the fill to the pressed color.
Render disabled as a neutral container with dimmed content (for example about 12% and 38% of the text color), not a pale tint of the accent.
Keep the button's width fixed while loading and block repeat presses.
Show the pressed state immediately on press (a transition of about 100ms or less), use about 150-200ms for hover, focus and color changes, and disable the motion under prefers-reduced-motion.
avoid: A pressed state that looks like disabled, a disabled state that looks enabled, or removed focus outlines.
Pale tinted focus halos, focus drawn only with box-shadow (forced-colors mode removes it), or a hover shade that drops the label below 4.5:1.
rules.note: Disabled buttons are exempt from contrast minimums but should stay legible; consider saying why an action is unavailable.

rules.title: Size buttons for touch and balance their padding
rules.why: Consistent height and padding make buttons easy to hit and visually balanced.
do: Make touch buttons at least 44pt (iOS) or 48dp (Android) tall; pointer-only interfaces can use 36-40px with an enlarged hit area.
Use roughly twice as much horizontal as vertical padding (for example 12-16px vertical, 24-32px horizontal).
With a leading icon, keep the full padding on the label side, take about 4-8px off the icon side (for example 16px and 24px) and use a 6-8px icon-label gap.
Set labels at about 14-17px on mobile in a medium or semibold weight.
avoid: Equal tiny padding on all sides, or primary buttons shorter than 44pt on touch screens.

rules.title: Make primary mobile buttons full width
rules.why: On narrow screens, full-width buttons are bigger targets and look finished.
do: Span the content width inside the platform side margins (typically 16-24px).
Stack paired actions vertically, with the secondary in a lower-emphasis style.
avoid: Small fixed-width buttons floating mid-screen, or buttons that touch the screen edges.
rules.note: On wide desktop layouts, size buttons to content or a max width instead.

rules.title: Place actions where the task ends
rules.why: Actions placed where the eye and thumb finish their path are found and reached faster.
do: On mobile, anchor the main forward action at the bottom of the screen, inside the thumb zone and above the safe area.
In forms, put the submit button directly after the last field, aligned with the fields, and keep it there on long scrolling forms on phones.

On short single-question phone steps, pin the forward action about 16px above the keyboard and safe area, with a keyboard-avoiding view natively or, on the web, a visualViewport resize listener or the viewport meta's interactive-widget=resizes-content.
In dialogs, align footer buttons the way the target platform does (where none applies, right-align them with the primary rightmost), and keep the order identical across the product.
In unsaved-changes dialogs, keep Save in the usual primary slot and move Discard to the far side in a low-emphasis style, so a habitual click never destroys work.
In quick-add lists, put the add button in the same row as its input and also submit on Enter, rather than below a list that pushes it down with every item.
avoid: The primary action as a small button in a top corner of a mobile screen, or button order that changes between similar screens.
rules.note: Primary-left versus primary-right ordering differs by platform; consistency matters more than either choice.

rules.title: Make the recommended option stand out
rules.why: Among similar items, the one that differs is noticed and remembered.
do: Give the recommended plan or default choice one distinct treatment, such as an accent border, a filled button or a "Recommended" badge.
Keep the other options visually quieter and emphasize only one item per group.
avoid: Emphasis by color alone, or emphasis used to push users toward an option against their interest.

rules.title: Make buttons look like buttons and links look like links
rules.why: Users expect buttons to act and underlined text to navigate; mixing the two causes mistakes.
do: Give primary and secondary buttons a filled or bordered shape with padding.
Make a tertiary text button a real button: a semibold accent label at 4.5:1 or more, no underline, button padding with a hit area at least 44px tall on touch, and a hover and pressed background.
Use button elements for actions and anchor elements for navigation, and reserve underlines for links.
If a soft extruded (neumorphic) style is required, add a border or fill step of at least 3:1 against the page and keep the label at 4.5:1.
avoid: Bare colored text with no padding or state feedback as an action, or an underlined link inside a row of action buttons.
Pressed or selected states shown only by a light-and-dark shadow pair on a fill that matches the page.

rules.title: Pair labels with a meaningful icon when it helps
rules.why: A recognizable icon beside the label speeds scanning.
do: Add a leading icon that matches the action (for example a phone glyph on "Call"), sized to the label line height.
Keep the text label and mark the icon aria-hidden.
avoid: Ambiguous icons, or icon-only buttons for uncommon actions.

rules.title: Show keyboard shortcuts on desktop actions
rules.why: A shortcut hint on the control teaches the faster path at the moment it is needed.
do: Render the shortcut as a small kbd chip inside or beside the button, styled quieter than the label.
Show the platform's modifier (Cmd on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere) and mirror it in the tooltip and aria-keyshortcuts.
In command palettes and launchers, keep a footer that names what Enter does for the highlighted item and which key opens more actions, and update it as the selection moves.
avoid: Shortcut chips on touch-only devices, or shortcuts documented nowhere in the UI.

rules.title: Explain unavailable actions instead of silently disabling them
rules.why: A plain disabled button cannot take focus and does not say what is missing.
do: Use aria-disabled="true" so the button stays focusable, and on activation move focus to the first invalid field.
Show a short live hint near the button that says what is still needed, and update it as fields become valid.
Let the primary label follow the state (Print, Re-print, Print next) and tint the suggested next action.
avoid: Disabled buttons with no explanation, or actions that stay clickable and fail silently.

rules.title: Keep the main action reachable
rules.why: A persistent, high-contrast primary action converts better than one buried in the hero.
do: Place the main action as a filled button at the right of a sticky header, paired with at most one quieter secondary in the hero.
Size any floating help or chat button at 48-56px with an accessible name, clear of content and safe areas.

On long mobile product pages, show a sticky bottom bar with the item name, price and main action once the hero action scrolls out of view, at least 56px tall plus env(safe-area-inset-bottom), with matching bottom padding on the page so it never covers the last content.
avoid: Several filled buttons of equal weight, or floating buttons that cover form fields or the last line of content.

rules.title: Give hover and press feedback without moving the hit box
rules.why: Subtle scale or lift confirms a target, but if the element under the pointer moves, hover flickers and clicks miss.
do: Use small changes (hover scale about 1.03-1.05, press about 0.95-0.97, card lift 2-5px) with ease-out: hover in over about 150-200ms and out slightly faster, press within about 100ms, and release over about 150-250ms with at most a slight overshoot, settled within about 400ms.
Animate an inner layer and keep the outer button or link box still.
Name the animated properties in transition-property and mirror the effect on :focus-visible.
Hide secondary row actions until hover only inside @media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine), reveal them on :focus-within as well, and keep them visible or in an overflow menu elsewhere.
avoid: transition: all, wobbly springs that take most of a second to settle, or hover as the only way to reveal an action.

rules.title: Write identity-provider buttons consistently
rules.why: Recognizable, consistently worded provider buttons speed sign-in without competing with the main path.
do: Use "Continue with <provider>" text with the provider's logo, at equal width and at least 48px tall on mobile, under an "or" divider.
Give every provider button the same height and fill treatment, using each provider's approved color variants, and signal any preference by order rather than by restyling one of them.
Follow each provider's button guidelines and give any icon-only variant an accessible name.
avoid: Unlabeled logo circles, one provider as a full button and the others as text links, or provider buttons styled louder than the primary sign-in when email is the main path.
rules.note: Platform sign-in guidelines require their button to be no smaller or harder to find than other providers' buttons.

rules.title: Put the amount in purchase buttons
rules.why: Showing the total inside the button makes the commitment explicit and removes a scan step.
do: Label purchase buttons with the verb and the exact amount ("Pay $248.00", "Add to order, $14.00") and update it as quantity changes.

When the price changes after the first quote, show the previous amount struck through and labeled as the old price, the new amount and the signed difference ("+$4.30"), and put the new amount in the accept button.
Place a quantity stepper beside it with labeled minus and plus buttons of at least 44x44px.
avoid: A generic "Continue" on the final charge step, or a button amount that disagrees with the summary or still shows an earlier quote.

rules.title: Add friction only for the riskiest choice
rules.why: Confirmation proportional to consequence protects users without slowing ordinary choices.
do: When the user selects the most severe option, reveal an acknowledgement checkbox that states the consequence in plain words, and keep the action aria-disabled (still focusable) and visibly unavailable until it is checked; if it is activated early, move focus to the checkbox and show a short live hint.
Relabel the action to describe the consequence and switch it to the warning style.
avoid: Confirmation steps on every option.
An action that looks the same before and after the acknowledgement is checked.

rules.title: Never make the decline option evasive
rules.why: Buttons that move away, shrink or cannot be pressed remove real choice and block keyboard, touch and motor-impaired users.
do: Give accept and decline stable positions and equal reachability, and differentiate them only by emphasis.
Set the decline option at body text size or larger, at 4.5:1 contrast, with neutral wording such as "No thanks".
avoid: A "No" button that jumps away on hover, or an "accept" option that grows each time the user tries to decline.
A tiny, faint decline link, or decline wording that shames the user.
rules.note: Acceptable only as an obvious joke in a toy; in consent, payment or account flows it is a dark pattern.

rules.title: Visible labels; placeholders only for examples
rules.why: Placeholder text disappears while typing and is usually low contrast, so it cannot replace a label.
do: Show a persistent label above every input, linked with label for/id.
Use the placeholder only for an example of the expected format (for example name@example.com), or leave it empty.
Give any placeholder at least 4.5:1 against the field fill and set ::placeholder { color: <secondary text token>; opacity: 1 }, because some browsers fade placeholders by default.
Put essential instructions in helper text below the field; since a placeholder dark enough to pass can look like an entered value, put the example there too or prefix the placeholder with "e.g.".
avoid: Placeholder-only labels such as "Enter email", including a leading icon (person, lock) with a placeholder, or a placeholder that repeats the label.
Placeholder, helper, error or success text below 4.5:1.
rules.note: A floating label resting inside an empty field is the field's only label, so it needs 4.5:1, and the floated label should stay at about 12px or larger; a static label above the field avoids both problems.

rules.title: Top-aligned labels in a single column
rules.why: Labels stacked above fields along one edge create a straight scan path that works at every width.
do: Stack each field full width with its label above it, aligned to the same edge as the submit button.
Let short related pairs (first and last name, city and postcode) share a row when space allows.
avoid: Unrelated fields side by side, or labels in a left column that force a zig-zag eye path on mobile.
rules.note: Left-aligned labels can suit wide desktop forms that must stay vertically compact.

rules.title: Group long forms under section headings
rules.why: Headings and spacing break long forms into chunks users can understand and complete.
do: Split long forms into titled groups (for example Personal information, Billing address, Change password) using fieldset/legend or real headings.
Make section headings clearly larger than field labels and leave more space between groups than between fields.
avoid: Seven or more unrelated fields in one undifferentiated column.

rules.title: Ask for less and let the product do the work
rules.why: Every field adds effort and abandonment risk; the system should absorb complexity it can handle.
do: Remove fields that are not needed for the task, and collect optional details later.
Prefer one full-name field over separate first and last name when the data model allows.
Prefill known data from the account or device, set autocomplete attributes, suggest addresses and reuse saved payment methods, keeping prefilled values visible and editable.
avoid: Asking again for information the product already has.

rules.title: Use the input type that matches the data
rules.why: Purpose-built inputs bring up the right keyboard, enable autofill and signal the expected answer.
do: Set type, inputmode and autocomplete (type="email", type="tel", inputmode="numeric", autocomplete="one-time-code").
Use one field for an email address, allow paste and trim whitespace before validating.

Let users type values they know instead of scrolling a long dropdown: enter a birth date as three short labeled fields (Day, Month, Year) with inputmode="numeric" and autocomplete="bday-day", "bday-month" and "bday-year", or as one field with the format in visible helper text and autocomplete="bday".

For phone numbers, pair a searchable country-code picker defaulted from the locale (autocomplete="tel-country-code") with a type="tel" national-number field (autocomplete="tel-national"), or use one autocomplete="tel" field that accepts a leading +; format as the user types and store the number in E.164.
Size fields to the answer: a single line for short values, a textarea for messages.
avoid: Email split into local part and domain boxes, or a one-line box for a long message.
Three dropdowns for a date of birth, or a date field whose only format cue is its placeholder.

rules.title: Choose the control by the kind of choice
rules.why: The control itself tells users whether one or many options can be chosen.
do: Use a visible radio group or segmented control for about 2-5 mutually exclusive options, and a select or combobox for long lists.
Use checkboxes for multi-select, a switch for on/off settings that apply immediately, and a single checkbox for yes/no choices submitted with a form.
Use chips for filters and tags, and labeled swatches for visual attributes such as color.
avoid: Hiding three or four short options in a dropdown, Yes/No in a dropdown, or checkboxes for mutually exclusive options.

rules.title: Type-to-filter for long lists
rules.why: Scrolling hundreds of items such as countries is slow; typing a few letters finds the item immediately.
do: Replace select menus longer than about 10 options (countries, time zones) with a combobox that filters as the user types and matches partial input, or put a filter field at the top of the list that takes focus when it opens.
Follow the ARIA combobox pattern: keep DOM focus in the input, move the highlight with arrow keys and aria-activedescendant, and let Escape close the list first and clear the text second.
Surface likely choices (for example the detected country) first, highlight the matched text, and announce the number of results in a polite live region.
Debounce lookups that call a server by about 150-250ms.
avoid: Hundreds of alphabetical options in a plain dropdown.

rules.title: Pair sliders with numeric inputs
rules.why: Sliders are fast for rough values but imprecise; people also need to see and type exact numbers.
do: Show the live value above the thumb or beyond the end of the track (not inside the track, where the thumb covers it), and label the minimum and maximum.
Increase values toward the trailing edge (right in left-to-right layouts, mirrored in right-to-left, up on vertical sliders) so the scale matches the arrow keys.
Pair the slider with editable number fields that stay in sync.
Prefer input type="range" with step (and a datalist for tick marks); give thumbs at least a 44px target and support arrow keys, Page Up/Page Down for larger jumps and Home/End.
Use a dual-thumb slider for ranges, name each thumb ("Minimum price", "Maximum price") and stop the thumbs from crossing.
In custom sliders, use setPointerCapture so dragging continues off the track, and touch-action: pan-y so vertical page scrolling still works.
avoid: A bare slider with no visible value, or a long dropdown of fixed numeric steps.

rules.title: Selectable tiles for a few comparable options
rules.why: When options differ by one or two key values, large tiles are easier to compare and tap than tiny radios.
do: For 2-6 options, lay out tiles with the main value bold (for example 1TB) and the secondary value below (for example the price).
Give unselected tiles a visible border (about 3:1 against the surface), and mark the selected tile with an accent border of 2px or more plus a round radio indicator or a check in a circle.
Keep radio semantics (role="radiogroup", arrow-key navigation, checked state).
avoid: Tiles for long or plain-text lists, or selection shown by a subtle color change only.
Square checkboxes on single-choice tiles, which suggest several can be chosen, or white tiles set off from a white surface only by a soft shadow.

rules.title: Design every field state
rules.why: Fields that change with state show users where they are and whether input is valid.
do: Define default, focused, filled, autofilled, read-only, disabled, error and success states.
Reserve a helper-text slot under each field so messages appear without shifting the layout.
Pair status colors with an icon and text, and keep success distinct from focus: mark validity with an icon and short text, and reserve border changes for focus and error.

Render read-only values with the readonly attribute so they stay focusable and selectable, keep their text at 4.5:1 or more, and show they cannot be edited by removing the border or tinting the fill; keep disabled styling for controls that cannot be used.
Style autofilled fields for each theme: browsers ignore background-color on :autofill (and :-webkit-autofill), so paint the fill with an inset box-shadow and set -webkit-text-fill-color for the text.
avoid: Disabled fields that look empty or enabled, or states shown by border color alone.
Read-only values greyed out like disabled controls, or a success border identical to the focus ring.

rules.title: Show specific errors inline, next to the field
rules.why: An error far from its field makes users hunt for the problem.
do: Validate a field first on blur or submit, show the message directly under the field with a red border and an error icon, and say how to fix it.
Once a field shows an error, re-validate on every input so the message clears as soon as the value is valid; raise new errors only at the next blur or submit.
Link the message with aria-describedby, set aria-invalid="true" and move focus to the first invalid field on submit.
Give the message text at least 4.5:1 with a darker error-text token (for example #DC2626 or darker on white); the brighter red can stay on the border and icon, which need 3:1.
Keep required and type for semantics but add novalidate when your script renders the inline messages, because the browser's validation bubble shows one field at a time and then disappears.
For new passwords, show a live checklist limited to length (at least 8 characters, or 15 when the password is the only factor) and "not a common or breached password".
avoid: A list of errors under the submit button, a generic "Error found" banner, or validating on every keystroke before the user has finished.
Flagging empty fields the user only tabbed through, or relying on the browser's built-in validation bubble.
rules.note: Sign-in is the exception: for wrong credentials show one generic message ("Email or password is incorrect") rather than marking a field, so the form never reveals which credential was wrong or whether the account exists.

rules.title: Mark required and optional fields one consistent way
rules.why: Users need to know what they can skip; clutter on every label slows them down.
do: When most fields are required, mark only the exceptions with "(optional)" inside the label element, in muted text that still reaches 4.5:1 (for example #767676 or darker on white).
Otherwise mark required fields with an asterisk and explain it once at the top of the form.
Always set required or aria-required on the input.
avoid: "(required)" in red on every label, or a symbol whose meaning is never explained.

rules.title: Show formats with hints and gentle masks
rules.why: Showing the expected format prevents errors before they happen.
do: Show patterns such as MM/YY or DD/MM/YYYY in persistent helper text or a mask, taking the date order from the user's locale (Intl.DateTimeFormat formatToParts) instead of hard-coding one.
Insert separators as the user types (card numbers in groups of four separated by single spaces, or 4-6-5 for 15-digit cards) and strip them before validating.
Keep the caret in place when reformatting by counting the digits before it, not characters, and size the field for the longest formatted value plus any icon, with tabular digits.
Accept pasted values in common formats.
avoid: Blank date or phone fields with no hint, or rejecting input because separators differ.
A caret that jumps to the end after an edit in the middle, or spaced hyphens between card-number groups.
rules.note: Masks must not block editing or confuse screen readers.

rules.title: Split long forms into steps with visible progress
rules.why: Short steps with a progress indicator reduce overwhelm and show how much is left.
do: Group about 3-4 related fields per step and show a stepper or progress bar.
End each step with a primary "Next" and a secondary "Skip" for optional steps.

Keep entered data when users move back or reload: put the step in the URL and keep the draft in sessionStorage, excluding card numbers, security codes, passwords and one-time codes, and clear it on submit.
avoid: Hiding how many steps remain, or splitting very short forms into many steps.
Saving payment or credential fields to localStorage or other persistent client storage.

rules.title: Use boxed fields, not underline-only fields
rules.why: Enclosed fields are recognized as editable and have a clear tap area.
do: Render inputs as outlined or filled boxes about 44-56px tall with a visible focus style.
Give the boundary that identifies the field at least 3:1 against the surface it sits on (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11), in both themes: about #949494 or darker on white, about #656565 or lighter on #18181B.
On filled fields whose fill cannot reach 3:1 against its surface, add a border or bottom line that does.
avoid: Bare underlines that look like dividers, or fields and code cells set apart from the card only by a soft shadow.
Faint borders or fills around 1.1-1.3:1 (for example #E5E7EB on white) on inputs; keep those for decorative card edges.

rules.title: Give rich-text editors familiar controls
rules.why: People writing formatted content should not need markup knowledge.
do: Provide a toolbar with bold, italic, underline, lists, link and image, plus a compact floating toolbar on text selection.
Explain where the content will appear and end with a secondary Cancel and a primary Save.
avoid: Raw markup for basic formatting in consumer-facing editors, or equally weighted Cancel and Save buttons.

rules.title: Build one-time-code entry that accepts typing, paste and autofill
rules.why: Codes arrive by keyboard, clipboard and OS autofill; boxes that only handle keystrokes force people to retype.
do: Prefer one real input styled as boxes, with inputmode="numeric", autocomplete="one-time-code", pattern="[0-9]*" and maxlength equal to the code length.

If separate boxes are unavoidable, put autocomplete="one-time-code" on the first box only, do not cap boxes at maxlength=1, and on the input event spread any multi-digit value (autofill or paste) across the boxes before moving focus.

Strip non-digits in the input handler (typing, paste and autofill alike), auto-advance on each digit, step back on Backspace in an empty box, and submit automatically only when exactly the expected number of digits is present (say so in the helper text).
Give the group a label (role="group" or fieldset) and each separate box a name such as "Digit 2 of 6"; drive the box count from one constant used in the copy as well.
For 6-digit codes, a small gap between two groups of three helps checking; draw it as an aria-hidden decoration, never as an extra box, character or tab stop.
Optionally request SMS codes with the WebOTP API (navigator.credentials.get with otp transport "sms").
avoid: type="number" (spinners, lost leading zeros), blocked paste, or a heading that says 4 digits beside 6 boxes.
maxlength=1 or single-character guards (such as /^\d?$/) on boxes that must accept autofill, the one-time-code hint repeated on every box, or a pasted code silently truncated into a wrong one.

rules.title: Wire sign-in fields for password managers
rules.why: Correct field semantics let browsers and password managers fill credentials, which removes most sign-in friction.
do: Use a real form with visible labels, type="email" with autocomplete="username" (or "email"), and autocomplete="current-password" on sign-in or "new-password" on sign-up.

In native apps set the hints for both platforms: textContentType for iOS (username on the email field, password or newPassword) and the Android autofill hint (autoComplete), plus keyboardType="email-address", autoCapitalize="none" and secureTextEntry.

When one view toggles between sign-in and sign-up, switch the password autocomplete, the confirm-password field and the submit endpoint together (or render two forms), and carry the typed email across; on sign-in the browser should offer saved logins, not a generated password.
Put "Forgot password?" beside the password field and state the duration on any "remember me" option.
avoid: Marking a sign-in password as new-password, or bare inputs with no type, label or autocomplete.

rules.title: Add a show-password toggle and keep password rules visible
rules.why: Revealing what was typed reduces errors, and rules that vanish on the first keystroke cause failed submissions.
do: Make the toggle a button type="button" inside the field's trailing edge with aria-label ("Show password") and aria-pressed, swapping the input type without moving the caret.
Keep rules such as "8 characters or more" in persistent helper text linked with aria-describedby, and accept at least 64 characters, paste and password-manager fill.

If you show a strength meter, pair the color with a text label, base its tiers on a pattern-aware estimator's guess count (dictionary words, names, dates, repeats, keyboard runs) rather than length times character-set size, and debounce the label so it is not announced on every keystroke.
avoid: A non-focusable eye icon, or rules stated only in the placeholder.
Composition rules (an uppercase letter, a digit, a symbol), or a meter that rewards character classes.

rules.title: Collect PINs and amounts with a clear keypad and a live readout
rules.why: Money and PIN entry need large keys, a visible value and a second check for invisible typos.
do: Show the amount large and centered with any converted value beneath it, updating on each key.

Prefer a native input with inputmode="decimal" (amounts) or inputmode="numeric" (PINs); if a custom keypad is required, use real buttons of at least 48px with labels for symbol keys and also accept hardware keyboards.
Mask PINs as filling dots, use autocomplete="new-password" for creation, and follow "Create PIN" with "Confirm PIN", clearing both and explaining on mismatch.
avoid: Echoing PIN digits in plain text, or a custom keypad as the only input path.

rules.title: Make upload zones state their limits and track each file
rules.why: Uploads fail in many ways; stating limits up front and showing per-file status prevents surprises.
do: Show accepted types, size limit and file count in the zone, and accept drop, paste and a real file input behind a visible browse button.

Switch the zone's border, tint and copy together as soon as dragenter fires, call preventDefault in dragover so drop fires, and count dragenter/dragleave (or set pointer-events: none on children while dragging) so the highlight does not flicker.
Word the drag-over state generically ("Drop 2 files to upload"), because file names and sizes are only readable after drop; pre-check types from DataTransfer.items where the browser exposes them.

List each file with name, size and its own progress bar, then done or failed with a reason and an inline Retry; freeze a failed bar at its last confirmed percentage and resume from the last acknowledged chunk where the upload protocol allows.
Show an aggregate summary ("3 of 4 uploaded, 1 failed") with clear and per-file remove controls that have accessible names.
avoid: Drag-and-drop as the only route, silent rejection, or failed files dropped from the list.
A highlight that fades in slowly behind the pointer, or restarting a broken upload from zero when it could resume.

rules.title: Write settings toggles as full rows that apply immediately
rules.why: Each switch should say what it does, take effect at once and be easy to hit.
do: Build each row as a label, a one-line description and a trailing switch (role="switch" with aria-checked, or a native checkbox styled as a switch), with the whole row as the target.
Show the on state by knob position and fill, not color alone, and give the off-state track a fill or outline of at least 3:1 against its surface in both themes (for example a 2px mid-gray outline).
Flip the switch at once with a small pending indicator in the knob until the server confirms; on failure move it back, restore aria-checked and say what happened near the row.
Offer undo or confirmation for security-sensitive changes.

When a page mixes instant toggles with fields that need an explicit save, say which group applies immediately, give the rest a sticky bar with an unsaved-changes notice, Cancel and Save, and warn before leaving with unsaved edits.
avoid: Switches with no visible label, or switches whose change only applies after a separate Save.
An off-state track so pale that it disappears into a light or dark card.

rules.title: Prefill quick-add forms with sensible defaults
rules.why: Option rows with realistic defaults let people create an item by typing one field.
do: Put the single required field first and focused, and show the other options as rows with an icon, label, current value and chevron that open pickers.
Choose defaults that cover the common case and show them as real values.

For new calendar entries, prefill the day selected in the calendar, start at the next half hour (or a morning time on future days) and end one default duration later; when the start moves, move the end by the same amount so the range cannot invert.
avoid: Turning every option into a required step, or chevron rows that are not tappable.

rules.title: Make date and time pickers show context and valid ranges
rules.why: Scheduling is easier when people see the surrounding week or month and cannot pick impossible ranges.
do: Use a week strip (day name above date, selected day filled, today marked differently) for near-term dates, with arrows for other weeks and a way to open a full calendar.
Bind the end date's minimum to the start date, use a two-thumb slider or paired fields for time windows, and echo the choice in plain words ("3 days, Fri 7 to Mon 10").
Define presets such as "Last 7 days" inclusively (today and the 6 days before) and show the resolved dates.
For date ranges, show two months side by side on desktop, and on phones a full-screen sheet of vertically scrolling months with a range summary and a sticky Confirm.
Give each day a full-date accessible name and aria-selected or aria-pressed, with targets of at least 40-44px.
avoid: Return dates earlier than pick-up dates, or selected days marked by color alone.

rules.title: Wire payment card fields for autofill and verification
rules.why: Autofill tokens and formatting cut card-entry time and errors.
do: Use autocomplete="cc-name", "cc-number", "cc-exp" and "cc-csc" with inputmode="numeric", group the number as the user types, and use one MM / YY expiry field that matches the card.

Show the detected network only once the prefix is unambiguous (some networks need up to six digits), with a neutral card icon until then, and report an incomplete number only after the field loses focus.
Explain the security code in helper text ("3 digits on the back, 4 on the front for some cards") rather than a "***" placeholder.
Prefer the payment provider's hosted fields, and label the pay button with the exact amount and a short security note.
Mark any live card preview aria-hidden and keep it out of the tab order; under reduced motion swap to the back face instantly instead of flipping.
avoid: type="number" for card numbers, or a decorative card preview as the only place the entered data is visible.
Separate month and year dropdowns for the expiry date.

rules.title: Show recent and saved values under search-like inputs
rules.why: Many entries repeat; showing recents removes typing entirely.
do: List recent or saved values (places, contacts, searches) under the field with an icon, bold name and muted detail, filtering as the user types.
Set enterkeyhint and suitable autocomplete values on the inputs.
avoid: Hiding recents until the user starts typing.

rules.title: Keep native semantics under custom-styled controls
rules.why: However decorative a slider, knob or switch looks, keyboard and assistive-technology users need it to behave like the real control.
do: Style the native element (input type="range" with appearance: none, a checkbox for switches), or use role="slider" or role="switch" with the matching aria-value or aria-checked attributes and full keyboard support.
Show the value as text with units and expose it through aria-valuetext ("96 dB, loud"), and keep thumbs at least 44px.
Communicate thresholds or danger zones with a label and marker, not only a color gradient.
Give unchecked checkboxes and radios a 1.5-2px border of at least 3:1 against the surface, and keep the check mark at 3:1 or more against the checked fill.
avoid: Div-only sliders or drag-only knobs.
Unchecked boxes or radios drawn as a pale, borderless fill.

rules.title: Verify on the server and send credentials only to your own backend
rules.why: Client-side checks can be bypassed, and generic form builders are not built to receive passwords.
do: Verify one-time codes, totals and permissions on the server, and post sign-in forms to your own authentication endpoint over HTTPS.
avoid: Hard-coded codes compared in client code, or passwords collected through a third-party form embed.

rules.title: Use one primary navigation pattern
rules.why: Combining navigation types splits destinations and makes the structure hard to learn.
do: On mobile apps, use a bottom tab bar with 3-5 top-level destinations.
Put overflow destinations such as settings into a Profile or More tab.
Keep the top bar for the screen title, search and notifications.
avoid: A hamburger menu on top of an existing tab bar, or primary destinations hidden in a drawer when a tab bar fits.
rules.note: A menu drawer is fine for secondary links; it lowers discoverability for anything important.

rules.title: Label every navigation icon
rules.why: Icons alone are ambiguous; labels make navigation predictable.
do: Show an icon plus a short text label for every tab, and color both when active.

Treat a bar that shows the label only on the active tab (an expanding pill) as icon-only for its inactive tabs: keep each one's accessible name (not removed with display: none) and give its icon at least 3:1 against the bar (NAV-03).
Size tab labels at about 10-12pt (never smaller) under icons of about 24pt.
Give icon-only controls elsewhere an accessible name and a tooltip.
avoid: Icon-only tab bars with abstract icons, or vaguely named menus.

rules.title: Make the current location unmistakable
rules.why: Users orient themselves by the active item; a weak active state leaves them lost.
do: Mark the active item with at least two cues: a tinted pill or indicator plus a bolder label or filled icon.

Use one accent color for the active item and one neutral for inactive items: inactive icons need at least 3:1, and every label, including an accent-colored active label, at least 4.5:1 (for example #707070 or darker on white or #F6F6F6).
When the active label turns bold, reserve its bold width (a hidden bold copy in ::after with content: attr(data-label), or a variable font's grade axis) so neighboring items do not shift.
Set aria-current="page" on the active link.
avoid: A different color for every nav icon, or a subtle color shift as the only active cue.
Fading inactive labels below 4.5:1 to make the active item stand out.

rules.title: Pick the navigation component that fits the scope
rules.why: Each component implies a different scope; the right one tells users where they are.
do: Use a tab bar or sidebar for top-level app sections, in-page tabs for views of one page, breadcrumbs for deep hierarchies and pagination for long result sets.

In pagination, highlight the current page, show previous/next arrows, render the first, last and current page with its neighbors with an ellipsis for skipped ranges, and compute the page count as ceil(total / pageSize); add a "Go to page" field for very long sets.

When in-page tabs overflow, scroll the row horizontally with edge fades (plus previous/next chevrons for pointer users) and keep the active tab in view; on phones switch to a section picker rather than shrinking tabs below 44px.
avoid: Tabs for sequential steps (use a stepper), or pagination without a current-page indicator.
Tabs wrapped onto a second row, or hundreds of page links.

rules.title: Breadcrumbs for deep hierarchies
rules.why: A visible path orients users and lets them jump up levels without repeated Back taps.
do: Show breadcrumbs on pages three or more levels deep.
Wrap an ordered list in nav aria-label="Breadcrumb" and link every crumb except the last; render the current page as plain text in the body text color with aria-current="page".
Draw separators with CSS (li + li::before) or aria-hidden elements so screen readers do not announce them.
On narrow screens, collapse middle levels into an ellipsis that expands on tap.
avoid: Breadcrumbs as a replacement for primary navigation, or on flat one-level sites.
A current crumb in the link or accent color, which reads as a link.

rules.title: Follow the conventions people already know
rules.why: People learn habits from many other products; familiar layouts need no relearning.
do: Put the logo top-left, inline with the main navigation, linked to home (mirrored for right-to-left languages).
Use conventional icons: magnifier for search, bell for notifications, house for home, person for profile, gear for settings.
Reuse standard gestures and behaviors such as swipe back and pull to refresh.
avoid: Novel icons for common concepts, or a centered logo above a separate row of links on content and product sites.
