rules.title: Put account and settings where people look for them
rules.why: People look for settings in a few conventional spots; anywhere else feels hidden.
do: In simpler apps, make the avatar in the header open profile and settings.
In larger apps, give Profile or More its own tab-bar item.
Keep the entry point in the same place on every top-level screen.
avoid: Settings reachable from only one screen or behind an unlabeled control.

rules.title: Structure sidebars top to bottom
rules.why: A predictable sidebar structure lets users orient themselves and switch sections quickly.
do: Order zones as logo with collapse toggle, optional search, main items under small section labels, secondary groups, settings and help, then the account or workspace switcher set off by a divider.
Use about 240px expanded width and a 64-80px icon rail when collapsed, with tooltips and accessible labels on every icon.
Use about 40px item rows with about 4px gaps, a consistent side inset of about 16px, about 24px between groups, and counts as right-aligned badges.
avoid: One long unlabeled list of links, or an icon-only rail without labels or tooltips.

rules.title: Limit sidebar nesting to two levels
rules.why: One expandable sub-level keeps related pages together; deeper nesting becomes hard to scan.
do: Let a primary item expand with a chevron to reveal indented second-level items, connected by a thin guide line.
Move deeper structure into in-page tabs or the page itself.
avoid: Third-level nesting inside the sidebar.

rules.title: Use the sidebar foot for at most one promo card
rules.why: The space below navigation is visible on every page without blocking tasks.
do: Place one compact card (usage meter with upgrade, trial offer or feature teaser) above settings and account.
Give it a close control, hide it in the collapsed rail and keep its button quieter than the page's primary action.
avoid: Several promo cards, or a card that pushes navigation out of view on short screens.

rules.title: Give tab bars full-size hit areas and safe-area padding
rules.why: Tab items need generous touch areas and must stay clear of the system home indicator.
do: Make each tab's hit area fill its whole column, with a 2-4px gap between icon and label.
Pad the bar's bottom with env(safe-area-inset-bottom) or the platform equivalent, and add bottom padding to the scroll content so the bar never covers it.
avoid: Labels sitting on the home indicator, or only the icon glyph being tappable.

rules.title: Expand search in place, with focus and an easy exit
rules.why: Folding search into an icon saves space only if the field opens instantly, takes focus and closes predictably.
do: Make the trigger a button with aria-label="Search" and aria-expanded; on activation expand the field over about 200-250ms and move focus into it.
Use input type="search" with a specific placeholder, a labeled clear button, and close on Escape or outside click with focus returned to the trigger.
Reserve or overlay the space so neighboring links do not jump, and optionally offer a shortcut such as / or Ctrl/Cmd+K with a visible hint.
avoid: Search that opens on hover only, or an expanded field covering links that stay tabbable underneath.

rules.title: Collapse sidebars without losing wayfinding
rules.why: A collapsed rail frees space, but people still need to see where they are and what each icon means.
do: Toggle with a button that has aria-expanded, aria-controls and a name that flips between "Collapse sidebar" and "Expand sidebar".
Keep the active highlight, section dividers and accessible counts in rail mode, with tooltips on hover and keyboard focus.
Animate width over about 200-300ms with icons in a fixed-width leading column so they stay put, and fade labels out first inside a column with overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap.
Persist the choice, and default to the rail on medium widths and an off-canvas drawer on phones.
avoid: Collapsed badges that become an unlabeled dot, or labels hidden with no tooltip or accessible name.
Icons that shift sideways, or labels re-truncated with an ellipsis on every frame, while the width animates.

rules.title: Derive the active item from the URL
rules.why: When the active state comes from the route, it can never disagree with what is on screen.
do: Use the router's link component (for example a NavLink) so the active class and aria-current="page" follow the current route.
Generate navigation items from one data array of name, path and icon.

Make hover and active look different so people do not lose their place while moving the pointer: give hover only a faint tint (about 6-10% of the text color) and keep the indicator, fill and semibold label for the current item.
avoid: A separate piece of state for the active tab that can drift from the URL.
A hover state identical to the current-page state, or a sliding hover underline that leaves no visible current location.

rules.title: Use navigation semantics for sections and tab semantics for panels
rules.why: Screen readers announce these differently, and each needs different keyboard behavior.
do: Use nav with links and aria-current="page" for app sections, including bottom tab bars.
Use role="tablist", role="tab" with aria-selected and aria-controls, a roving tabindex and arrow keys only for in-page panels.

Select tabs as focus moves when panels render instantly, and only on Enter or Space when panels load slowly; support Home and End, let Tab move into the panel (tabindex="0" on a panel with nothing focusable), and draw focus as a ring distinct from the selected indicator.
avoid: role="tablist" with no tab panels, or tabs built from divs with click handlers.

rules.title: Hide bars on scroll only with a threshold
rules.why: Hiding navigation while reading down and restoring it on scroll up gives content room without losing wayfinding.
do: Hide the bottom or top bar after a meaningful downward scroll (about 10px or more) and restore it on any upward scroll or at the top.
Hide the bar over about 200-250ms and bring it back faster (about 150ms), and let content extend under the bar so the layout does not jump.
Keep the title bar pinned (position: sticky) and keep labels on the restored bar.
avoid: Toggling the bar on tiny scroll jitters.

rules.title: Open submenus as disclosures, not hover traps
rules.why: Nested sections must open for keyboard and touch users and stay open while the pointer crosses gaps.
do: Make the parent a button with aria-expanded controlling a list of links, visually attached to its parent, opening on click, Enter and Space, staying open while focus or the pointer is inside, and closing on Escape and outside click.

For pointer users, keep the submenu open while the pointer moves toward it (a safe triangle toward the submenu, or a close delay of about 300ms), and close it promptly once the pointer leaves that path.
Highlight the current child item.
avoid: Hover-only flyouts that collapse when the pointer crosses a gap.
A collapsed navigation that expands only on hover, which hides every link from touch and keyboard users (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.1.1 and 1.4.13).

rules.title: Keep the user's place in long lists
rules.why: Returning from a detail view to the top of a list, or to a page whose rows have shifted, forces people to find their place again.
do: Choose the paging style by task: numbered pages for reference data people jump through, "Load more" when the footer must stay reachable, infinite scroll only for feeds.
Keep page, cursor, sort and filters in the URL (?page=, ?after=), and use cursor (keyset) pagination when rows are added while people browse.

On Back, restore the scroll position and focus to the row the user opened (save the item id and offset in history.state or sessionStorage; in virtualized lists scroll to the id), and briefly highlight it.
Keep each tab's scroll position when people switch between tabs.
avoid: Resetting scroll to the top after Back, or offset pages that repeat or skip rows when data changes.
Infinite scroll on pages whose footer holds needed links.

rules.title: Make touch targets at least 44pt
rules.why: Small hit areas cause missed taps, especially on icon-only controls.
do: Make every tappable element at least 44x44pt (iOS) or 48x48dp (Android).

Keep icons visually small if desired (about 24px) and enlarge the hit area with padding or an invisible overlay; on the web, @media (pointer: coarse) { .icon-btn { padding: 12px } } turns a 20px glyph into a 44px target.
Give text buttons and links a full-height hit area even when the text is small.
Re-check every control's hit area after a spacing or density pass; extra whitespace can still leave steppers and chips below 44pt.
avoid: Hit areas that match a 16-24px glyph exactly, such as back, close, favorite or password-visibility icons.
Controls that need a hover state before they work; on touch, a first tap may only apply the hover style.
rules.note: WCAG 2.2 sets 24x24 CSS px as the AA minimum and 44x44 as enhanced; platform guidance asks for 44pt/48dp.

rules.title: Space touch targets so taps land where intended
rules.why: Crowded targets cause mis-taps; the smaller the target, the more space it needs.
do: Keep hit areas from overlapping and leave at least 8px between adjacent 44-48px targets.
For targets smaller than 24x24 CSS px, apply the WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 spacing test: a 24px circle centered on each target must not intersect another target or another target's circle.
avoid: Tiny icon buttons packed edge to edge or against screen edges.

rules.title: Keep key actions in the thumb zone
rules.why: In one-handed use the bottom of the screen is easiest to reach.
do: Anchor the main forward action (Continue, Next, Pay) at the bottom of the screen above the safe area; in multi-field forms put it directly after the last field instead, pinning it above the keyboard only on short single-question steps (BTN-05).
Add bottom padding to scroll content so a sticky action never covers the last field.
Keep destructive or rarely used actions out of the easiest reach zone.
avoid: Critical actions as small targets in the top corners.

rules.title: Respect safe areas
rules.why: Content under the status bar, notch or home indicator is obscured or collides with system gestures.
do: Read insets at runtime: env(safe-area-inset-top/bottom) on the web, with viewport-fit=cover in the viewport meta tag (without it iOS reports 0), SafeAreaView or platform APIs in native code.
Keep the top navigation row clear of the status area and leave the home-indicator zone free of controls, including when the keyboard is open.
avoid: Hard-coded inset values from one device; top insets range from about 20pt on home-button phones to about 59pt or more on phones with a camera cutout.

rules.title: Use consistent side margins
rules.why: A fixed horizontal margin keeps content aligned and away from screen edges.
do: Apply the same page margin on every mobile screen, typically 16-24px, and align headers, titles and grids to it.
Let only intentional full-bleed elements such as images and carousels break the margin.
avoid: Text or cards touching the screen edges, or different margins on different screens.

rules.title: Design for the full range of phone sizes
rules.why: Phones vary widely in width and height; layouts must adapt without per-device tweaks.
do: Verify layouts from about 320pt to 440pt wide and on short screens.
Use fluid widths, flex and grid rather than fixed pixel layouts.
Check that primary actions and key content are not pushed off-screen on short devices.
avoid: Designing for one device size and assuming it scales.

rules.title: Use horizontal rows with a peek for browsable sections
rules.why: Horizontally scrolling rows let users see more categories without a long vertical scroll.
do: Lay out each category as one horizontal row under its heading, with the next card partly visible to signal more.
Use scroll snapping and offer a "See all" route.
avoid: Rows whose cards fit the viewport exactly, hiding that more content exists.
rules.note: Content in carousels is easy to miss; put the most important items first.

rules.title: Keep push notifications rare and useful
rules.why: Too many or irrelevant notifications lead people to disable them or uninstall the app.
do: Send only notifications with clear value, written short and specific, and targeted to the relevant users.
Let users control categories and frequency, batch updates and respect quiet hours, giving each notification type its own channel or category so it can be muted on its own.

Replace an outdated alert instead of stacking a new one (the same apns-collapse-id on iOS, the same notification tag on Android, since an FCM collapse_key only merges undelivered messages), and group related alerts (thread-id on iOS, setGroup with a summary notification on Android).
avoid: Bursts of near-identical notifications or generic marketing pushes to everyone.

rules.title: Keep forms clear of the keyboard and system bars
rules.why: On phones the keyboard covers half the screen, and inputs under it or the status bar break forms on real devices.
do: Wrap native forms in a keyboard-avoiding container (padding behavior on iOS; adjustResize usually covers Android) around a scroll view with keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled", so the first tap on Submit works while the keyboard is up, and pad the bottom with the safe-area inset or at least 16px (Math.max(insets.bottom, 16)).
Chain fields with a "next" return key and make the last field submit.

On the web, let the form scroll and use scroll-padding with env(safe-area-inset-*) so the focused field and the submit button stay visible; an action pinned on a single-question step sits about 16px above the keyboard (BTN-05).
avoid: Fixed-height centered columns that cannot scroll when the keyboard opens, or hard-coded status-bar heights.

rules.title: Give small custom controls a real role and a larger hit area
rules.why: Tiny checkboxes and inline links are hard to hit and invisible to screen readers without roles and state.
do: Extend hit areas with padding or hit slop of (target size - visual size) / 2 per side, for example 12-14px around a 16-20pt checkbox for 44pt, or make the whole label row the target, so they reach 44pt (iOS) or 48dp (Android) and never fall below 24x24px (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8).
Give custom checkboxes accessibilityRole="checkbox" with a checked state, or use a native checkbox with a label, and make the label part of the same target.
avoid: A checkbox built from a plain view with only a press handler, or a tappable square whose label is not tappable.

rules.title: Always pair gestures with a tap alternative
rules.why: Swipe, hold, slide and drag gestures are undiscoverable for some people and impossible for others.
do: Label both outcomes of a swipe as real buttons (for example "False" and "True") and support arrow keys.
Reserve slide-to-confirm and press-and-hold for rare, deliberate commitments and also accept tap-then-confirm or Enter; a slide-to-pay control states the exact amount (BTN-14).

Make holds clearly longer than the system long press but short (about 0.8-1.5s, never several seconds) with a ring that fills in proportion; on early release drain it back and say nothing happened, and cancel on pointercancel or when the pointer leaves.

For swipe rows, let a short swipe reveal actions without firing them and a long swipe past most of the row commit only the outermost action, signalled before release; keep each revealed action at least 44px wide and destructive actions on the trailing side.
For press-and-hold recording, respond on touch-down with feedback that extends beyond the fingertip, offer slide to cancel and a lock for long recordings, and also allow tap to start and tap to stop.
Add a short hint near any non-standard gesture ("Pull and release").
avoid: Swipe-only answers, slide-only buttons for routine actions, or drag as the only way to complete a task.
rules.note: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA) requires a single-pointer alternative to any drag.

rules.title: Respond to every action immediately
rules.why: Silence after a tap leaves users unsure whether anything happened, so they tap again.
do: Acknowledge input within about 100ms with a pressed state or an optimistic change (keep Interaction to Next Paint at 200ms or less), then show a busy state (for example a spinner and "Saving...") while work runs.
Disable the control while the request is in flight to prevent double submits.
Confirm the result explicitly, success or failure.
avoid: A button that looks unchanged while a request runs in the background.
rules.note: About 100ms feels instant; past about 300-400ms show a busy state in place (the control disabled with progress text, as in FBK-10), and add a standalone spinner or progress bar only past about 1s (FBK-02).

rules.title: Match the loading indicator to the wait
rules.why: The right indicator reassures users without flashing or lying about progress.
do: Show nothing for waits under about 300ms, a busy state in place from there, a spinner with a short label past about a second, and skeletons for content-shaped loads.

Once an indicator appears, keep it for about 400-500ms so a reply just after the delay does not flash it; if it became visible, await the request and the minimum time together (for example Promise.all([request, minVisible])).
Use a determinate bar or ring with a percentage when progress is measurable.
Draw spinners as an open arc or a ring with a visible gap; a uniform ring shows no motion when it rotates.
When refreshing content already on screen (search as you type, filters), keep the previous results visible, replace rows in place and signal the refresh with a thin progress line.
Mark loading regions with role="status" or aria-busy.
avoid: An indefinite spinner for an operation whose progress is known, a bar that fills and resets in a loop for one whose progress is unknown (use a moving segment or a spinner), or a progress bar with no label.
Clearing a list to show a centered spinner while new results load.

rules.title: Confirm outcomes with clear status messages
rules.why: Users need to know whether an action worked, failed or needs attention.
do: Use distinct success, error and warning variants, each with a tinted background, a matching icon and plain wording.

Set message text in the dark step of the status hue or in neutral text so it reaches 4.5:1 on the tint (for example #166534 on #DCFCE7, about 6.5:1), and keep the brighter status color for the icon (3:1 against the tint) and the border.
Say what failed and what to do next (for example "Couldn't save your changes. Try again.").
Put decision buttons inside warning banners when a choice is needed, and expose messages with role="status" or role="alert".
avoid: Completing an action with no visible change, or generic errors without a next step.
Mid-tone status text on its own tint (#16A34A on #DCFCE7 is about 3:1), or one phrase of the message recolored in the status hue.

rules.title: Use toasts for confirmations, not for errors that need work
rules.why: Toasts disappear; anything users must act on needs to stay visible.
do: Show short success toasts with an icon, a title and one line, pausing the dismiss timer on hover or focus.

Scale auto-dismiss with length and weight: about 4-5s for a one-line confirmation, about 7-10s for warnings or toasts with an action, and no auto-dismiss for errors or for actions available nowhere else (WCAG 2.2.1).
Keep at most about 3 toasts visible, newest nearest the anchor edge, anchored clear of navigation and never over the middle of the content, and allow swipe to dismiss on touch.
Announce toasts through an ARIA live region and give them a close control.
Keep errors that need action inline or in a persistent banner.
avoid: Important information that exists only in a toast.
Toasts for routine navigation or for results the screen already shows.

rules.title: Show steps in multi-step flows
rules.why: Seeing which steps are done, current and left reduces anxiety and drop-off.
do: Show 3-6 named steps: completed steps with a check, the current one highlighted, upcoming ones muted.
Mark the current step with a heavier weight, the primary text color and aria-current="step", and add a text equivalent ("Step 3 of 5: Payment").
Mute upcoming steps through weight, outline markers and number style while keeping their text at 4.5:1 and their markers and connectors at 3:1; they are information, not disabled controls.
If the stepper also shows a bar or percentage, compute it from completed steps and reach 100% only after the final submit succeeds.
Let users go back to completed steps.
avoid: States told apart by color alone, or hidden step counts.

rules.title: Show progress toward goals
rules.why: People are more motivated the closer they see themselves to a goal.
do: Show progress bars with visible text naming the value and the goal for goals, profile completion and long tasks (for example "Step 2 of 4" or "700 of 1,000 points, 70%").
Build them with <progress> or role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin and aria-valuemax, drawn as a plain fill.
Give an honest head start where the user has genuinely made progress.
avoid: Raw numbers with no visual indicator, or invented progress.
A knob or thumb on a progress bar, which reads as a draggable slider.

rules.title: Design the high point and the ending
rules.why: People judge an experience mostly by its most intense moment and how it ends.
do: Make completion screens clear and warm: an icon or illustration, a headline, a short summary and a useful next action.

Match the success surface to the stakes: a short toast with Undo for reversible changes, a persistent confirmation page or receipt (items, amount, masked card, date) for payments and orders, and a status tracker with timestamps (Sent, Opened, Paid) when the real outcome comes later.
Celebrate real milestones briefly, with a full-size Continue or Close visible from the first frame, a tap anywhere skipping to the end state, and sharing kept secondary.
avoid: Ending a long flow with a blank page or silent redirect, or placing upsells and extra forms at the final step.
A celebration that holds back the way forward or offers it only as a small, faint link.

rules.title: Make destructive confirmations unmistakable
rules.why: Destructive dialogs must say exactly what will be lost and which button does what.
do: Title the dialog as the action on the named object ("Delete Q3 Report?"), show a warning icon, and repeat the name in bold in the body with its scope (how many items it holds, who loses access).

Label buttons with explicit outcomes ("Keep project", "Delete project") and style the destructive one red and the safe one neutral, using a red that gives its white label at least 4.5:1 (#DC2626 is about 4.8:1; #EF4444 fails at about 3.8:1).
Put initial focus on the safe action, let Escape cancel, and never let a backdrop click confirm (CMP-12).
For unsaved changes, offer three outcomes: Save (primary), Discard (a low-emphasis destructive style, placed away from Save, as in BTN-05) and Cancel to keep editing.
Offer undo, or require typed confirmation for high-impact irreversible actions.

For typed confirmation, show the exact name in monospace beside the field, allow paste, enable the button only when the trimmed input matches, label it with the consequence ("Permanently delete <name>"), and list what else disappears.
avoid: Generic Yes/No buttons with identical styling.

rules.title: Turn empty states into a first step
rules.why: An empty screen is a dead end unless it explains what belongs there and how to start.
do: Show a specific headline ("No projects yet"), one or two lines on what will appear and why it helps in text that meets 4.5:1, and one primary action that starts it.
Offer templates, examples or import options where relevant, and keep navigation visible.

Write different messages for "nothing created yet", "no search results" (clear the search, check spelling), "hidden by filters" (how many items are hidden, with Reset filters) and "failed to load" (with a retry).
avoid: A bare "No data" message on a blank screen, or several competing buttons.
Faint gray supporting text, or an empty collection presented as an error code such as "404".

rules.title: Show progress inside the button for async actions
rules.why: Feedback in the exact place the user clicked prevents double submits and doubt.
do: When the wait passes about 300ms, swap the label for a present-progressive verb with a spinner ("Signing in...", "Placing order...") or a percentage for measurable work.
Set aria-busy and block re-submission from the first press, and keep the button width fixed while the label changes.
On success show a short confirmation state ("Added" with a check) for about 1.5-2s; on failure restore the button and show an inline error.
Keep the form mounted and readable while it submits: make the fields read-only, and on failure keep the values and move focus to the field that needs fixing.

If a progress fill sweeps under the label, layer an on-accent copy of the label clipped to the filled part (clip-path driven by the same progress variable, marked aria-hidden) so every glyph keeps its contrast.
avoid: Spinner-only buttons with no text, or buttons that stay active during the request.
Replacing the form with a loader, or hiding it with opacity alone, which leaves its fields focusable; make any covered form inert (ENG-05).

rules.title: Never show success for consequential actions before the server confirms
rules.why: A success animation that runs on a timer can contradict what actually happened, especially for payments and orders.
do: For payments, transfers, orders, bookings and irreversible changes, start processing visuals when the request starts and show the verdict only when the real result arrives.
Treat only a 2xx response (response.ok) as success: send 401 to re-authentication, show 409 and 422 as inline field errors using the server's messages, and offer Retry for 5xx and network failures.
Design the failure path as carefully as success: distinct label, color and icon, and a retry.
Let animations celebrate a change that already happened, never delay the state change itself.
avoid: Fixed setTimeout waits before or instead of the real request, or treating any response with a body as success.
rules.note: Low-risk reversible actions may update optimistically if they roll back visibly on failure (FBK-21).

rules.title: Report progress honestly
rules.why: Progress that jumps backwards, races ahead or keeps moving during a stall erodes trust.
do: Drive determinate progress from real work (for example bytes read from response.body.getReader() against Content-Length) and keep it monotonic.

Keep the printed percentage equal to work done, rounded down and held at 99 until the done event (Math.min(99, Math.floor(p * 100))), since rounding shows 100% at 99.5%; to make updates feel smooth, ease only between real values (about 200-300ms ease-out per update).
Keep the bar indeterminate when the total is unknown, never show 100% before the work is finished, and show a stalled state if nothing arrives for about a second, leaving the bar where it stopped.

For transfers longer than a few seconds, show done and total, rate and time left ("12 s left, 1.8 MB/s"), computing time left from a moving average over the last few seconds, hiding it for the first second or two and rounding to coarse units ("A few seconds left").
Expose role="progressbar" with aria-valuenow once determinate, show percent text, and offer Cancel (for example through AbortController).
avoid: Fixed-duration or front-loaded fills unrelated to the work.

rules.title: Give code verification explicit states
rules.why: After the last digit, people need to see that the code is being checked and what happened.
do: Move through entering, checking (digits stay visible and locked, aria-busy on the code field, a spinner beside it), verified (success color, check, next step) and error (message plus icon).

On error, show the message at once, keep the wrong digits visible for about half a second, then clear them and return focus to the code field (its first box if the boxes are separate inputs, FRM-17); keep the message until the user types again.
Keep any shake to about 300-400ms, 2-3 cycles and 8px or less, and drop it under reduced motion.
Announce state changes through a polite live region, using role="alert" for the error.
Keep the resend countdown running after an error and stop it once verification succeeds.
avoid: Signaling the result with glow color or a shake alone.
Replacing the code field with a loader while checking.

rules.title: Keep the app shell steady while content loads
rules.why: Blank flashes and full-page spinners between views jolt the eye and hide the layout.
do: Keep navigation and headers mounted and swap only the content region, using skeletons at the real sizes and positions.
Delay any spinner by about 300ms so fast loads show nothing, match the current theme's background, and set aria-busy on the loading region.

Hide skeleton blocks from assistive technology (aria-hidden) and give the region a visually hidden "Loading <thing>" status; animate any shimmer with a transform on a pseudo-element over about 1-1.5s in reading direction (mirrored for right-to-left), static under reduced motion.
Replace a skeleton with an error and Retry on failure or after a timeout (for example about 10s).
Reserve space for images and charts (aspect-ratio, fixed heights) so nothing shifts when data arrives.
Render new content as soon as its data is ready, with at most a 150-250ms opacity or translate entrance.
avoid: A white loading screen inside a dark app, or blur-in effects after the data is ready (animated blur across whole sections is also costly to render).

rules.title: Prefer undo over confirmation for reversible deletes
rules.why: An undo window is faster than a dialog and still protects against mistakes.
do: Remove the item immediately, update counts, and show a status toast ("Deleted brand-assets.zip") with Undo and a visible countdown, committing when it expires.
Keep the undo window at about 7-10s (FBK-04), pause it on hover, focus and while the page is hidden, and make Undo a full 44x44px target.
Back the toast with a soft delete (a deleted_at timestamp) and a Trash that keeps items restorable for a stated period such as 30 days, so the toast is not the only way back.
Restore undone items at their original position, and name the target in icon-only delete buttons.

For messages that cannot be recalled once delivered, hold the send for an adjustable grace period (about 5-30s) with a seconds countdown and an Undo that returns the draft to the editor, and commit on the server when the timer ends so closing the tab neither loses nor duplicates it.
avoid: Modal confirmations for actions that can be undone, or undo windows too short to reach.

rules.title: Confirm add-to-cart without interrupting
rules.why: Shoppers want proof the item was added and a path to the cart, not a modal that ends browsing.
do: Update the cart count at once (optimistically or on the add response), never when a fly-to-cart animation lands, switch the add button to "Added" briefly, and announce it at the same moment through a polite live region.
Show a toast or a persistent "View cart" pill with the count, keeping any toast for at least about 4-5s (FBK-04) and pausing it on hover or focus.
Restart the confirmation timer on every add (clear the previous timeout, or key the toast to the current count) so a quick second add is not hidden early.
avoid: Forcing a cart drawer or page open on every add, or confirmations shorter than a second.

rules.title: Name the state of long-running and sensing tasks
rules.why: For background jobs, voice input and camera capture, users need to know whether the system is working, listening, done or stuck.
do: Show a distinct status line per state (working on step X, listening, thinking, done, failed with retry), with the indicator animating only while active.
Give the status line body-text contrast (4.5:1); if streamed text fades in, fade only the newest words and bring them to full contrast within a few hundred ms.

Drive typing and thinking indicators from real events, clear them a few seconds after the last one, and label automated replies as such; never simulate typing or add a delay before a result that is already available.

For capture tasks, give live positioning guidance or an input-level meter, warn that the microphone may be muted after about 2s of near-silence, show numeric progress, and offer manual entry or upload as a fallback.
Mirror changes in a polite live region; give toggles such as a microphone a fixed name with aria-pressed, or an action label that changes, never both.
avoid: Animation or color as the only sign that a microphone is live or a job failed.

rules.title: Make exceptions stand out with more than color
rules.why: In monitoring and operational lists, out-of-range records must be visible at a glance.
do: Give exceptions a strong treatment plus an explicit text or icon marker, and offer a filter or sort that brings them to the top.
Show "last updated" times for live data and briefly tint newly arrived rows.
avoid: A red fill as the only signal, or small white text on saturated red without a contrast check.

rules.title: Keep splash screens and preloaders honest and short
rules.why: A launch screen only earns its delay if it reflects real loading.
do: Tie any progress to real asset loading, finish within about 1-2s, continue automatically and let users skip.

Keep the native launch screen until the first screen has rendered (hide it from a first-frame callback, not at process start) and give the root window the first screen's background, so no blank frame flashes between them.
Show a brand intro at most once per session.
avoid: Fake percentage counters that hold back content that has already loaded.

rules.title: Keep interface sounds opt-in
rules.why: Unexpected audio is disruptive, especially in shared spaces.
do: Keep UI sounds off by default, provide a visible sound toggle in a consistent place, and remember the choice.
Give the toggle a constant name ("Sound") and expose its state with aria-pressed and an icon that changes.
avoid: Playing sound on load or on the first interaction without an obvious control.
A label that flips between "Sound on" and "Sound off" while aria-pressed also changes, which announces the state twice.

rules.title: Update low-risk actions optimistically and roll back visibly
rules.why: Waiting for the server on likes, toggles or sent messages makes a fast product feel broken, but an optimistic change that silently reverts misleads people.
do: Apply reversible, high-success actions (like, follow, save, toggle, reorder, send message) locally at once, keeping the previous state and a pending marker.
On failure restore exactly the previous state and say what was reverted, with Retry ("Couldn't save, change undone").
Coalesce rapid repeats into the latest intent and ignore responses older than the last request (ENG-02).
Keep payments, transfers, permanent deletions and bookings on server-confirmed states (FBK-11).
avoid: Optimistic success for money, permissions or irreversible changes.
Silent rollback with no message, or a spinner in front of a low-risk action.

rules.title: Handle lost connections with a persistent status and automatic retry
rules.why: An outage is an ongoing condition, so a dismissable toast or a blocking dialog either hides it or traps the user, and blind retries can overload the server.
do: Show a persistent, non-modal banner (role="status") while offline or degraded, driven by failed requests as well as the online and offline events, and clear it with a brief "Back online" once requests succeed.
Retry automatically with exponential backoff and jitter (about 1, 2, 4, 8s, capped near 30s), show when the next attempt happens ("Retrying in 3s") and offer "Retry now".
Keep typed input and queued actions, mark unsent items as pending, and send them after reconnecting.
avoid: Auto-dismissing toasts or modal dialogs for an outage that is still happening.
Fixed-interval retry loops, or discarding the user's draft on a network error.
rules.note: Give queued writes an idempotency key so a retry after a lost response cannot apply them twice.

rules.title: Give time-limited decisions a visible clock and a safe outcome
rules.why: Offers, holds and sessions that expire silently or under unseen time pressure cause missed choices and lost work.
do: Show the time left as text ("14 s", "Hold ends in 4:59"), optionally with a shrinking bar, computed from the deadline timestamp (ENG-09), and say what happens at zero (offer declined, seats released).
Give accept and decline equal size and reach, and on expiry return to a stable state with a status line ("Offer expired, still searching") instead of a blank screen or an error.

For limits the user did not choose (sessions, cart or seat holds), warn at least 20s before expiry and let them extend with one simple action (WCAG 2.2.1, which exempts real-time events such as auctions).
avoid: Countdowns on choices with no real deadline (false urgency), or limits that end without warning.
Announcing every second to assistive technology; announce only at thresholds such as 10s left (ENG-09).

rules.title: Set foundations before drawing screens
rules.why: Settling color, type, spacing, radius and elevation scales first prevents one-off values and keeps screens consistent.
do: Define tonal ramps for the brand hue and a neutral gray, a 5-6 step type scale, a 4- or 8-based spacing scale, and small radius and elevation scales.
Build screens only from those scales.
avoid: Choosing values ad hoc screen by screen.

rules.title: Layer tokens and name them by purpose
rules.why: Referencing named decisions instead of raw values lets one change propagate everywhere and makes theming possible.
do: Use three tiers: primitives (blue-500 = #2563EB), semantic tokens (color-action-primary) and component tokens (button-bg-default).
Name semantic and component tokens by purpose, not appearance (button-primary, not blue-button).
Pair every fill token with an on-color token (color-action-primary with color-on-action-primary) and remap each pair together.
Rebrand by changing primitives and support dark mode by remapping the semantic tier per theme, using the same names in code as in design files.

Test the token set after every change: size tokens increase with their names, spacing values sit on the scale and every text and fill pair still meets contrast; if white text drops below 4.5:1, point the fill at a darker step (600-700) or switch the on-color to near-black.
avoid: Hex, spacing or radius values hard-coded inside components.
Assuming a new primitive keeps the old contrast.

rules.title: Build a few core components completely
rules.why: A small, fully specified set covers most screens and stays maintainable.
do: Start with button, input, card, avatar and navigation.
Give each explicit variants (primary, secondary, ghost, destructive), sizes (sm, md, lg) and states (default, hover, pressed, focus, disabled, loading).
Step sizes evenly (for example sm, md and lg at 40, 48 and 56px tall) and extend anything under 44px to a 44px hit area on touch screens.
Build one configurable Button component (variant, tone, size, leading or trailing icon, icon-only, badge) instead of styling buttons per screen.
avoid: Dozens of half-finished components, or components that only have a default state.

rules.title: Document how each component is used
rules.why: Short, consistent documentation turns a library into a shared language for design and code.
do: Give each component one page: when to use it, do and don't examples, properties and accessibility requirements (target size, the focus ring's color, width and offset, and the actual contrast ratio of each variant and state rather than a checkmark).
Record version, status and owner, and keep release notes.
avoid: Shipping or changing components without usage guidance or a changelog.
Unchecked accessibility claims, such as "meets 4.5:1" on a fill that reaches only 3.1:1.

rules.title: Pick one radius scale that fits the brand
rules.why: Corner rounding sets the tone, and a consistent scale makes components feel like one system.
do: Choose one tier and store it as tokens: sharp (0-2px) for formal products, moderate (4-16px) for neutral ones, or pill (height/2) for friendly ones.

Apply it consistently and scale it with component size, for example about 4px for chips and badges, 6-8px for buttons and inputs, 8-12px for cards, 12-16px for dialogs and sheets, 999px for pills, and about 2-6px in dense data UI.
Set corners that touch a viewport edge, such as docked sheets and sidebars, to 0 on that side.
avoid: Sharp, rounded and pill buttons mixed on one screen without a reason.
One medium radius (about 12-16px) on every element regardless of its size.

rules.title: Keep nested corners concentric
rules.why: An inner element with the same radius as its container leaves an uneven gap at the corners.
do: Set inner radius = outer radius - padding (a 24px card with 8px padding gets a 16px inner radius).

Use a small or zero inner radius when padding is equal to or larger than the outer radius; if the result looks too sharp, raise the outer radius or reduce the padding instead of inflating the inner radius.
Apply the rule outward for rings: a focus or selection ring offset 2px around an 8px corner needs a 10px radius (outline follows border-radius, but box-shadow and pseudo-element rings need it set).
Crop media that sits flush with the card edge with overflow: hidden on the card instead of giving the image its own radius.
avoid: The same radius on a card and the image inset inside it.
Halving the outer radius as a shortcut, which is concentric only when the padding is half the radius.

rules.title: Keep elevation soft and consistent
rules.why: Dark, tight or overused shadows look heavy and dated; soft, consistent elevation separates layers cleanly.
do: Use low-opacity, diffuse shadows with blur about twice the offset and no horizontal offset, for example 0 8px 24px rgba(15,23,42,.08), tinted toward the background hue rather than pure black.
Define a few elevation tokens (sm, md, lg) and reserve the strongest for floating layers such as menus, popovers, dialogs and drag previews.

When more than a few resting elements in one view would carry shadows, separate them with a tone step or a 1px light border instead, using one method for every card in a set, so a shadow still means "above the page".
avoid: Default heavy black shadows on every card and button, or shadows and strong borders on the same element.

rules.title: Size components to their content
rules.why: Content-driven sizing keeps padding consistent when labels change or are translated.
do: Let buttons hug their label plus fixed padding, fixing only the dimension that must stay constant (such as height).
Use flex or grid gaps for lists and cards so repeated items keep consistent spacing.
Use full width only where the layout calls for it, such as a bottom action on mobile.
avoid: Fixed button widths that clip longer labels, or absolute positioning that breaks when content changes.

rules.title: Same look, same meaning
rules.why: Elements that look alike are read as related, so visual treatments must map consistently to meaning.
do: Style every element with the same function identically: one button style per emphasis level, one link color, one chip shape.
Use one shared component for parallel items such as pricing tiers, and emphasize the recommended one with a single deliberate variant.
Group items that share a state together (for example unread items first).
avoid: Reusing a highlight style for unrelated purposes, or letting heading and icon colors drift between sibling cards.

rules.title: Give segmented controls an inset track
rules.why: An inset track makes segmented options read as one control.
do: Wrap the options in a track with about 4-8px inset, and show the selected option as a raised or contrasting pill with at least 3:1 against the track (WCAG 1.4.11) plus a weight or icon change.
Over imagery, give the track a near-opaque tint and draw the selected pill in a solid contrasting fill.
Give each option button-like padding and keyboard support.
avoid: Segmented options placed directly on the page background with no track.
A translucent selected pill on a translucent track.

rules.title: Keep tooltips short and reachable without hover
rules.why: Brief contextual help explains a control without cluttering the layout, but hover-only help excludes touch and keyboard users.
do: Show tooltips on hover after about 500-700 ms and at once on keyboard focus; while one is open, show neighbors without the delay for about 300 ms.

On touch, use a long press or, better, a visible label; for standalone info icons use a toggletip, a button with aria-expanded that opens the text on tap or click and closes on Escape or an outside tap.
Meet WCAG 1.4.13: Escape dismisses without moving pointer or focus, the tooltip stays open while the pointer moves onto it, and it stays until hover and focus leave or the user dismisses it.
Keep the text to a 1-4 word label or one or two short sentences, at most about 240-320px wide, anchored to the trigger with an arrow and flipped to stay inside the viewport.
Link descriptive tooltips with aria-describedby, give icon buttons an aria-label matching their tooltip, and give first-run hints an explicit "Got it".
avoid: Essential instructions that exist only in a tooltip, or interactive content inside tooltips.
Tap-to-show tooltips on controls whose tap performs an action, or hiding the tooltip as soon as the pointer leaves the trigger.

rules.title: Use modals for focused tasks and popovers for light context
rules.why: Blocking overlays interrupt; they should be reserved for tasks that need full attention.
do: Use a modal (scrim, trapped focus, visible close, Escape to dismiss, Cancel plus one primary action) for focused edits, preferably the native dialog element opened with showModal(), which provides the top layer, an inert page and Escape handling.
In destructive confirmations, put initial focus on the safe action, ignore backdrop clicks and name the object in the title and the button ('Delete "Q3 plan"?', "Delete plan").
Use a non-blocking popover anchored to its trigger for short contextual content, dismissed by an outside click or Escape.
Return focus to the trigger when either closes.
avoid: Blocking overlays for trivial information, or dialogs with no visible way out.

rules.title: Give avatars fixed sizes and fallbacks
rules.why: Avatars personalize the interface, but missing photos must never break the layout.
do: Use a fixed size scale (for example 24, 32, 40, 48, 64px).
Fall back from photo to initials to a generic person icon, and place status badges at the bottom-right, scaled with the avatar.
Add a 2-4px ring in the surface color when an avatar overlaps a photo or another avatar.
avoid: Broken-image icons or arbitrary avatar sizes per screen.

rules.title: Structure action menus
rules.why: Account and overflow menus stay scannable when items are grouped and the exit action is isolated.
do: Open with a header that identifies the context (avatar, name), then group related items with dividers and leading icons.
Show shortcut hints right-aligned on desktop, and place Sign out or destructive items last in their own group.

Follow the menu keyboard model: arrows move, Home and End jump, a typed letter jumps to the next matching item, Right opens a submenu, Left or Escape closes only that submenu, and Escape at the top level closes the menu and returns focus to the trigger.

Give right-click menus a touch route (a long press of about 500 ms, plus a visible overflow button) that opens the same actions in the same order in a bottom sheet titled with the item's name, and flip menus opened at the pointer to stay inside the viewport.
avoid: A long undivided list, or Sign out mixed into everyday items.
Actions reachable only by right-click.

rules.title: Make cards self-contained modules
rules.why: One topic per bounded card makes feeds and dashboards scannable and lets them reflow responsively.
do: Give each card one topic: a title, one key value, supporting metadata and at most one or two actions.
Keep padding, radius and separation identical across sibling cards.
avoid: Unrelated data or several competing buttons in one card.

rules.title: Make selected items obvious
rules.why: A small checked box alone is easy to miss in a list.
do: Change the whole row when selected (accent fill or tint, stronger border) and keep a check or checkbox as a non-color cue.
avoid: A selected row that looks identical to unselected ones except for a tiny checkbox.

rules.title: Give KPI tiles a fixed anatomy
rules.why: Dashboards are scanned tile by tile; a fixed structure makes every number interpretable at a glance.
do: Order each tile as a small label, a large value with tabular numerals, then a delta with arrow, sign and comparison period ("+4.9% vs last month"), giving every tile its period.
Add a sparkline only when the trend's shape matters for that metric, and an icon only when it speeds recognition between otherwise similar tiles.
Mark up each tile as a labeled pair (dl with dt and dd, or the label as its heading), and keep the sign in the delta text because arrow icons are usually aria-hidden.
Render tiles from a data array of raw values mapped to one component, formatting with Intl.NumberFormat at render time (signDisplay: 'exceptZero' shows no change as a neutral "0%").
Derive the arrow from the delta's sign and its color from a per-metric higher-is-better flag, since falling churn or cost is good news.
State changes in rate metrics (conversion, churn) in percentage points ("+1.1 pp vs last month", not "+1.1%"), keeping relative percentages for counts and amounts.
Add a hover lift only when the tile opens a detail view, and give it a focus style too.
avoid: Up or down shown by green and red alone, hover lift on non-interactive tiles, or preformatted strings that cannot be sorted.
An icon in a tinted circle and a sparkline on every tile by default, or a bare number as the tile's heading.

rules.title: Make charts answer one question and reveal exact values
rules.why: A chart is only useful if the reader knows what it shows, over what period, and can read exact values.
do: Give each chart a title, a one-line summary, a time-range control and labeled axes, and highlight the current or key series while muting the rest.

Default line charts to straight lines about 2px wide, without area fill unless the area means something (such as a cumulative total), markers on every point or smoothing that draws values between samples.
Keep lines, markers and other meaningful marks at least 3:1 against the plot background in every theme (WCAG 1.4.11), with separate stroke tokens per theme.
Show exact values in tooltips on hover and keyboard focus, put the total in the center of donuts, and list values beside legend entries.
Provide a text or table alternative and wrap charts in a responsive container.
avoid: Color-only legends, tiny low-contrast axis labels, glossy or 3D bars that distort comparison, or entrance animations replayed on every refresh.

rules.title: Build operational tables for triage
rules.why: Lists are read by status and recency; those must be scannable without decoding.
do: Use real table markup with th scope="col", right-aligned numbers with tabular numerals, and status pills with words.
Add filter tabs with counts above the table, show relative times with the absolute timestamp in a time element, and highlight the selected row with aria-selected beside a detail pane.

Keep rows to one line: show a missing value as an en dash with visually hidden text ("No due date"), and truncate long text with an ellipsis and the full value on hover and focus, but never truncate numbers.
Offer density presets (rows about 40, 48 and 56px tall, at least 48px where rows are touch targets), separate rows with a hairline and a hover tint, and keep zebra stripes for very wide tables.
Pin the header (top: 0) and identifying columns (left: 0) with position: sticky, an opaque background and an edge shadow once scrolled, setting overflow only on the table's own scroll wrapper.
Put row actions in a visible overflow button, revealing frequent ones on hover and :focus-within for pointer devices, and mark only the active sort column with an arrow and aria-sort.
Switch layout with a container query on the table's wrapper, and when rows become cards use list markup or restore table roles, since changing display on table elements can drop their semantics.
avoid: Column widths that jump when the selection changes, or status shown by a colored dot alone.
Blank cells for missing values, or a pencil-and-trash column on every row.

rules.title: Give list rows a leading visual, two lines and a trailing value
rules.why: A consistent row anatomy makes transactions, devices and people lists scannable.
do: Place an avatar, logo or icon first, primary text above secondary text, and the key value right-aligned at the end.
Keep signs on money values (-$24.00, +$240.00) with tabular numerals, group long lists under date headers, and keep tappable rows at least 48px tall.

When a table collapses into rows on a phone, put identity and the right-aligned amount on line one and the status pill and a labeled date ("Due 12 May") on line two, and replace the lost column headers with a sort control.
avoid: Red and green as the only difference between debits and credits, or truncated trailing values.

rules.title: Keep product cards comparable
rules.why: Uniform cards let shoppers compare quickly across a grid.
do: Use a fixed image aspect-ratio with object-fit: cover, then category, name, price (right-aligned or accent), rating with its count, and one add action with an accessible name that includes the product.
Make the title the card's link and keep the add button outside the link; use grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)) for the grid.
avoid: Price or the add action shown only on hover, varying image heights, or nested interactive elements.

rules.title: Give carousels controls, position and a pause
rules.why: Rotating content hides information, so people need control over it.
do: Provide labeled previous and next buttons, a position indicator ("3 of 8"), keyboard arrows and scroll snapping.
Pause on hover and focus and offer a pause control if anything autoplays; treat 3D coverflow as optional styling over the same controls.
Drive drag, buttons and arrow keys through one fractional position that springs to the nearest item on release, and derive each item's scale and opacity from its distance to that position.
avoid: Autoplay without a way to stop it, drag as the only way to move, or the only copy of critical information inside a carousel.

rules.title: Give segmented controls and chips real selection semantics
rules.why: Compact toggles are fast, but assistive technology must know what is selected.
do: Use native radios or role="radiogroup" with role="radio" and aria-checked for single choice, and toggle buttons with aria-pressed or checkboxes for multi-select chips.
Move selection with arrow keys using a roving tabindex, and show the selected state with fill plus a check or weight change.

Style the selected state from the ARIA attribute itself ([aria-checked="true"], [aria-pressed="true"]) instead of a separate class, so what is drawn cannot drift from what is announced, and keep that plain style until any script-drawn indicator has painted.
Let horizontal chip rows scroll with the last chip peeking past the edge.
When a toggle chip carries its own menu, place the menu button beside it as a sibling with its own name and at least a 24px target, never inside it.
avoid: A radiogroup role around plain buttons with no radio roles, ARIA roles without the matching keyboard behavior, or a faint tint as the only selected cue.

rules.title: Make swatch pickers named radio groups
rules.why: Swatches are single-choice inputs and must be operable and named like one.
do: Build them as a radio group, give each swatch a text name, and mark the selected one with an offset ring plus the visible variant name.
Keep the hit area at least 44px even when the visible dot is small, and update an accent token so the whole product view reflects the choice.
avoid: Unnamed color dots, or a per-variant accent that fails contrast on its background.

rules.title: Keep the current selection visible and removable
rules.why: People should always see what they picked and be able to undo it without reopening a menu.
do: Show the selected value in the trigger, or as a chip with a labeled remove button.
Announce changes in a polite live region and use listbox or menu semantics with Escape returning focus to the trigger.
avoid: Replacing the labeled trigger with an unlabeled icon once a value is chosen.

rules.title: Route accents through one token per theme or variant
rules.why: When every accent use reads one custom property, re-theming and per-item colors stay consistent.
do: Define the accent once (for example --accent) and set it per theme or variant with a data attribute, using it for text, fills, borders, glows and focus.
Check each variant's accent against its own background.
avoid: Repeating accent hex values across many rules.

rules.title: Use a large fixed radius for pills
rules.why: A fixed large radius keeps semicircular ends at any width, while 50% turns wide elements into ellipses.
do: Use border-radius: 999px for pills, chips, pill buttons and indicators.
avoid: border-radius: 50% on non-square elements.

rules.title: Prefer the native share sheet
rules.why: The system share sheet lists the user's own apps; a custom icon row is only a fallback.
do: Call navigator.share when navigator.canShare allows it, and otherwise expand a row of labeled share targets plus "Copy link" with immediate confirmation.
avoid: Unlabeled brand icons, or a share row that opens on hover.

rules.title: Give feeds and notifications a fixed item anatomy
rules.why: A predictable order makes long feeds and notification lists scannable.
do: Show avatar, name, relative time and an overflow menu with an accessible name, then body text clamped to 2-3 lines with an in-place "See more", then media and reactions with counts.
For notifications, put the actor in bold, the action text and a relative time, entering with a short slide and fade.
avoid: Wrapping a card that contains buttons in one big link, or autoplaying video with sound.

rules.title: Lay out media players in the familiar order
rules.why: Familiar control order lets people operate a player without hunting.
do: Show artwork, title and artist, a progress bar with elapsed and total time, then shuffle, previous, a larger play or pause, next and repeat.
Give icon buttons accessible names and reflect toggles such as shuffle and repeat with aria-pressed.
avoid: A play button the same size and weight as the secondary controls.

rules.title: Build checklists from real checkboxes with a live count
rules.why: Clear done states and a running tally give a sense of progress.
do: Use labeled checkboxes, show done items with a check, line-through and reduced emphasis, and update "3 of 8 completed" in a polite live region.
Name delete buttons after their item and offer undo.
avoid: Deleting with no undo, or low-contrast placeholder text on dark surfaces.

rules.title: Lay out receipts and money summaries for checking
rules.why: Financial summaries must be easy to verify line by line.
do: Use label and value rows with tabular numerals and right-aligned amounts, listing subtotal, discount (with a minus sign), fees, tax with its rate and a bold total, plus a reference number.
Render receipts as real text that can be selected, printed or downloaded.
avoid: Marking discounts by red alone, or decoration that covers the figures.

rules.title: Give drag and drop a lift, a landing preview and a non-drag path
rules.why: Moving items by drag is predictable only when people can see what they hold, where it will land and whether the drop is allowed, and some people cannot drag at all.
do: On pickup, lift the item within about 150-200 ms: a grabbing cursor, scale about 1.02-1.05, a stronger shadow and optionally a tilt of 3 degrees or less, dropped under reduced motion.

Preview the landing spot with a placeholder the size of the item at the drop position (an insertion line in dense lists), a tint for whole-container drops, and outlines of valid slots on snapping grids.
Enforce limits during the drag: show counts such as "3 / 4" in group headers and refuse a drop into a full group with a reason ("Column is full, 4 of 4").
Announce pickup, position and drop in a live region, and offer Undo for about 5-10 s after a drop.
Provide a single-pointer alternative such as a "Move to…" menu or move buttons (WCAG 2.5.7), plus a keyboard mode: Space to lift, arrows to move, Space to drop, Escape to cancel.
avoid: Moves that persist silently with no landing preview or undo, or a flat ghost that looks as if nothing was picked up.
Drag as the only way to reorder or move items between groups.

rules.title: Encode quantities by position or length, not area or radius
rules.why: People compare positions and lengths accurately but misjudge areas, and a circle whose radius doubles covers four times the area, so radius-scaled circles exaggerate every difference.
do: Compare values with bars from a zero baseline, dots on a shared axis or lines; sort bars by value unless the categories have a natural order such as months.
When a circle must carry a value, such as bubbles on a map, scale its area rather than its radius and print the value beside it.
Use a gauge or progress bar only for one value against a known target or range, and show the target.
avoid: Nested or concentric circles, radial bars or 3D shapes for comparing totals such as yearly revenue.
Dot-matrix or segmented bars whose dots cannot be counted and whose exact values are not available on focus or in a table.
rules.note: A pie or donut is acceptable for two to four parts of one whole when every part is labeled with its value.

rules.title: Keep live event feeds readable while they update
rules.why: A feed that inserts rows while someone reads or clicks moves the target under the pointer and floods screen readers.
do: Hold new events while the user is scrolled away from the top or interacting with a row, and show a "12 new events" button that loads them.
Give each operational event a severity word and icon, one line on what happened, the affected asset and an absolute timestamp with time zone, newest first, with relative time as a secondary label.
Offer Pause and Resume, and show the connection state and last update time ("Live · updated 09:24:18 UTC").
Announce only important events, batched, in a polite live region ("3 new critical events"), never every row.
avoid: Auto-scrolling the list, re-sorting it while a row has focus, or severity shown by color alone.

rules.title: Use one icon family and one style
rules.why: Mixed icon styles look assembled from scraps and can make one icon seem selected.
do: Use a single icon library with one style (outline or filled), one stroke width for the whole product (for example 1.5 or 2) and one size grid (for example 20 or 24px), optically centered.
Size icons from the adjacent text, about 16px beside 14px labels and 20px beside 16px text, and nudge directional glyphs such as play and arrows about 1px toward their point so they look centered.
If filled icons mean "active", apply that rule to every item.
avoid: Filled and outline icons, or different stroke widths, in the same bar or list.

rules.title: Use conventional icon metaphors
rules.why: Familiar icons are recognized instantly; novel metaphors make users guess.
do: Use widely understood icons: gear for settings, sliders for filters, bookmark for save-for-later, paper plane for send, lock for privacy, globe for language, a play triangle for resume after pause and a circular arrow only for retry or refresh.
Add a text label wherever an icon could be ambiguous.
When one button toggles between states (pause and resume), swap the icon and the accessible name together ("Pause upload", "Resume upload").
Reserve trailing chevrons for rows that open a deeper level, and mark an option chosen in place with a check instead.
avoid: Custom metaphors for common actions, or an icon that conventionally means something else.

rules.title: Add leading icons to long settings and navigation lists
rules.why: A familiar icon beside each label is a second cue that makes long lists faster to scan.
do: In long settings and navigation lists that people scan by category, place one 20-24px icon from the same set at the start of each row, in a single aligned column.
Keep the text label and mark decorative icons aria-hidden.
avoid: Long text-only settings lists, or icons that replace the label.
Decorative icons on short lists, table rows or every label in a form.

rules.title: Give icon-only controls a name
rules.why: Screen readers and new users cannot interpret an unlabeled glyph.
do: Give every icon-only control an aria-label and a tooltip with the same text.
Prefer visible labels for primary navigation and uncommon actions.
Include any visible text in the accessible name, ideally at its start (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3 Label in Name), and mark decorative alternate words shown on hover aria-hidden.
avoid: Unnamed icon buttons, names that differ from the visible tooltip, or controls that reveal their label or destination only on hover, which touch users never see.

rules.title: Use imagery that supports the message
rules.why: Images that do not illustrate the message add noise; relevant visuals speed understanding.
do: Choose images or illustrations that show what the headline promises, in a style consistent with the brand.

When no real imagery exists, prefer in order: your own photographs of the product, the real interface rendered with believable data, drawings of the product's own objects in its palette, then type and color alone.
Keep content backgrounds calm and let product imagery provide the visual interest.
avoid: Generic stock photos as filler, or decorative blobs and shapes behind product grids and text.
Generic 3D characters, isometric people or generated scenes that do not depict the product, or stock and generated pictures passed off as photos of the actual product, premises or staff.

rules.title: Crop images to keep the subject visible
rules.why: Cropping that cuts off the subject makes a card lose its meaning.
do: Use object-fit: cover with object-position set to the subject's focal point, and check crops at each breakpoint.
avoid: Stretched images (object-fit: fill) or automatic center crops that cut off faces or products.

rules.title: Normalize SVG strokes for progress and scaling
rules.why: A few SVG attributes keep line weights stable when graphics scale and make progress strokes trivial to drive.
do: Set pathLength="1" and drive stroke-dasharray and stroke-dashoffset in 0-1 units for rings, borders and draw-on lines.
Add vector-effect="non-scaling-stroke" to strokes in responsively scaled SVGs, and transform-box: fill-box on parts that rotate or scale around their own center.
Start rings at 12 o'clock with a -90 degree rotation and round line caps.
avoid: Calling getTotalLength every frame, or a solid spinning ring for something that is not loading.

rules.title: Switch from outline to filled for active icons
rules.why: Swapping an outline icon for its filled version is a clear, low-cost state change.
do: Use outline icons at rest and the filled version only for the selected or active state, with the label weight increased; show hover and :focus-visible with a color or background tint of the same glyph instead.
Transition only the properties that change (color, opacity, transform) for about 200-300ms.
avoid: transition: all, or hover animation as the only sign of interactivity on touch devices.
Filling icons on hover, which makes the hovered item look selected, or swapping a line icon for a full-color illustration on hover, which mixes two styles in one row.

rules.title: Ship a still fallback for animated illustrations
rules.why: Animated illustrations can fail to load or need pausing; a still frame keeps the page meaningful.
do: Include a static image of the key frame alongside any Lottie or canvas animation, with the alt text on one of them and the other aria-hidden.
Show the still when scripts fail or prefers-reduced-motion is set.
avoid: An empty box until the animation library loads.

rules.title: Generate repeated SVG parts in code
rules.why: Radial or repeated details are easier to tune when generated in a loop than drawn by hand.
do: Create nodes with document.createElementNS("http://www.w3.org/2000/svg", "rect"), rotate each by i * 360 / count, build once, then animate the group with one transform.
Draw evenly spaced ticks with one circle and a dash pattern where possible.
avoid: document.createElement for SVG elements (they land in the HTML namespace and do not render), or one DOM node per tick when a dash pattern would do.

rules.title: Keep pixel art crisp
rules.why: Default smoothing blurs pixel art and bitmap-style lettering.
do: Set image-rendering: pixelated on scaled sprites and canvases and scale by whole-number factors.
avoid: Fractional scaling of pixel assets, or pixel fonts for body text.

rules.title: Do not use emoji as interface icons
rules.why: Emoji render differently on every platform, ignore color tokens and stroke weights, and are read aloud by their names, so they rarely fit the rest of the interface.
do: Use one vector icon set for navigation, buttons, bullets, status and feature headings, or no icon at all.
Keep emoji where they are user content: reactions, messages, names and user-chosen labels.
If an emoji must appear as decoration, wrap it in an element with aria-hidden="true" and keep the meaning in visible text.
avoid: Emoji in navigation items, buttons, headings, list bullets or empty states.
An emoji as the only carrier of a status or meaning.

rules.title: Label buttons with the outcome
rules.why: A verb that names the result tells users exactly what will happen.
do: Use verb plus object: "Save changes", "Add to basket", "Delete project", "Pay $12.96".
Keep the label consistent with the screen title and the confirmation message.
avoid: "Yes", "No", "OK", "Submit" or "Done" when a specific verb exists, or a bare noun as a label.

rules.title: Keep button labels on one line
rules.why: Wrapped button text looks broken and gets worse on small screens and in translation.
do: Write labels of 1-3 words and test at the narrowest supported width (320px) and in long languages.
Shorten the copy or let the button go full width instead of wrapping.
avoid: Labels that break onto two lines, or shrinking the font below the standard button size.

rules.title: Write labels in plain language
rules.why: Internal or marketing jargon confuses users who have never seen those terms.
do: Name settings by their effect ("Hide balances", "Help and support"), and be specific with legal links ("Privacy policy", "Terms and conditions").
Use standard wording for account actions: "Log out", "Close account".
Phrase toggle labels as the state that turning them on produces.

In headlines and value statements, replace genre words (unlock, supercharge, seamless, next-generation, all-in-one) with a specific noun, number or outcome; if a competitor's name could be swapped in and the line still works, rewrite it.
avoid: Team-internal feature names, single vague nouns, or the same word for two different rows.
Slogan formulas such as three one-word sentences or "Not just X, it's Y".

rules.title: Keep confirmations short
rules.why: People skim, so brief messages are understood faster.
do: Use one or two words for routine confirmations ("Saved", "Copied") next to the relevant icon.
Add detail only when users need it to decide or act.
avoid: Full exclamatory sentences for simple confirmations.

rules.title: Ship no placeholder copy
rules.why: Leftover template words are the first thing users notice and they undermine trust.
do: Search the UI and code for "Title", "Button", "Label", "Text", "Lorem ipsum" and similar strings before shipping.
Run a spell-checker over the UI string files in CI, and read each page's copy against that page's topic to catch text pasted from elsewhere.
Seed demos and fixtures with plausible names, units and dates, and totals that equal the sum of their rows.
avoid: A checkout card headed "Title" with a button labeled "Button".
Round vanity figures, or demo tables whose totals do not add up.

rules.title: Avoid all-caps labels
rules.why: Mixed case keeps word shapes recognizable, so it reads faster and feels calmer.
do: Write labels in sentence case or title case and apply one convention across the product.
Keep source strings in natural case and set text-transform: none on buttons.
avoid: All-caps primary buttons or long all-caps labels.

rules.title: Say where the code went and when it can be resent
rules.why: Naming the destination and the wait prevents duplicate requests and doubt about the address used.
do: State the code length and the masked destination ("4-digit code sent to ••• 0142") with a link to change it.
Keep "Resend" visibly unavailable during a cooldown with a live label ("Resend in 0:24"), using aria-disabled so it stays focusable and explains the wait (BTN-10), and enable it at zero.
Announce only when resend becomes available, not every second.

Keep the destination sentence, the resend prompt, the countdown and any security note at 4.5:1 or better even while the Resend control looks unavailable, since they are information, not the disabled control; if the code expires on a different clock from the cooldown, label each timer ("Expires in 4:59", "Resend in 0:24").
avoid: Hiding the resend option until the timer ends, or styling enabled and disabled resend identically.

rules.title: Format numbers with the viewer's locale everywhere
rules.why: Mixed separators make amounts ambiguous (99.560 next to 14,867).
do: Format every number, currency and date through Intl with the viewer's locale (account setting or navigator.language), applied consistently within a view, including chart axes, tooltips, tables, slider readouts and their aria-valuetext.

Take the currency code from the data and let the currency style place the symbol and set the decimals: new Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { style: 'currency', currency: record.currency }) gives $4,500.25 for en-US, 4.500,25 € for de-DE and no decimals for JPY.
Use compact notation ("$164.4K", "$5.05M") for axis ticks and donut centers, letting the formatter choose K, M or B, and full precision in tooltips and details.

Write dates with a named month through Intl.DateTimeFormat (for example { day: 'numeric', month: 'short', year: 'numeric' }), or as ISO 8601 (2025-12-05) in technical contexts, and pick plural nouns with Intl.PluralRules ("1 step", "18,839 steps").
avoid: Hand-built number strings, toFixed() for money, mixed decimal marks, or currency symbols on some values but not others.
A hard-coded locale, numeric-only dates such as 05-12-2025, or K or M appended to an already grouped number ("$5,050K").

rules.title: After success, relabel with the outcome or the next step
rules.why: A button that still says "Send" after sending invites a second click.
do: Switch to a past-tense confirmation ("Sent", "Added", "Downloaded") with a check, or to the obvious next action ("Open file").
Make the confirmation visually quieter than the original call to action.
avoid: Leaving the original verb in place after success.

rules.title: Translate raw numbers into consequences
rules.why: People act on outcomes ("safe for 2 hours") more than on units ("91 dB").
do: Pair a technical value with a plain-language consequence and a status word (Quiet, Loud, Danger), computed from a documented model.

Name the model in the interface; for sound exposure, the NIOSH limit allows 85 dBA for 8 hours and halves the time for every 3 dB above it (about 38 minutes at 96 dB), with no limit shown below 85 dB.
avoid: The raw number alone, or alarmist copy the model does not support.

rules.title: State offer conditions up front
rules.why: Deals feel trustworthy when dates and limits are visible before the click.
do: Show the discount with a one-line benefit, its validity dates or channel limits, and a link to the terms.
Show the original price struck through (s or del) beside the new one and the saving.
avoid: Conditions hidden in fine print after the click, or "limited time" claims that keep reappearing.

rules.title: Make trust and data-safety statements specific
rules.why: In finance and data products, concrete statements about access and control build trust before people connect accounts.
do: Use a few short cards, each with an icon, a 2-3 word title and one specific sentence (for example read-only access, encrypted connections, how to disconnect).
Place them next to the step that asks for access.
avoid: Vague security claims, or low-contrast gray body text in those cards.

rules.title: Show ratings with their scale and sample size
rules.why: A bare star count is not believable; scale and count are.
do: Show the rating with its scale (4.9/5) and a real count of reviews or users, and link to the reviews.
Give outcome percentages and averages their base nearby: how many people, and when ("92% of 1,240 members surveyed in 2025").
Compute the average from the actual distribution and round it to one decimal the same way wherever it appears.
avoid: Ratings with no scale or count, percentages with no base or date, or invented figures; drop any claim you cannot back up.

rules.title: Explain unusual interactions in two or three words
rules.why: When a control is not a standard button, a tiny instruction prevents confusion.
do: Place a short, quiet instruction beside the affordance ("Pull and release", "Hold to confirm") and provide a click or keyboard alternative.
avoid: Relying on users to discover a gesture with no hint.

rules.title: Offer fewer, clearer choices
rules.why: Decision time grows with the number and similarity of options.
do: Show only the options most users need at each step and move the rest behind "More" or "Advanced".
Mark a recommended default and give options short distinguishing subtitles.

Collapse fine-grained ranges into a few buckets that place every possible value in exactly one: 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6+ for whole numbers, half-open wording for continuous quantities ("Less than 1 year", "1 to under 3 years", "3 years or more").
avoid: Long flat lists of near-identical options, or every setting on the first screen.
Ranges that share endpoints (1-3, 3-5), or integer ranges for values that can fall between them.

rules.title: Put key items first and last
rules.why: People remember the first and last items of a sequence best; the middle is the weakest spot.
do: Lead lists, onboarding and landing sections with the strongest benefit or most-used item.
Place the most important action at the end of a sequence.
avoid: Burying essential information or actions in the middle of a long list.

rules.title: Chunk information without hard caps
rules.why: Grouped information is easier to scan and remember than one undivided mass.
do: Group related items under headings or spacing, keeping each visible group small.
